Why Red Sox Could Pursue Japan Triple-Crown Winner Seeking Move To MLB This Offseason originally appeared on NESN. Add NESN as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
If there's one thing the Red Sox need to add to their lineup this offseason, it's power.
Boston ranked 26th among all MLB teams — and third-to-last among squads that made the postseason — in home runs this past season, hitting 163 as a unit with Willson Contreras' 27 leading the way. Against the Yankees in the AL Wild Card series, the Red Sox had just four extra-base hits over two games.
There are a number of names who could be available, whether through free agency or via trade, that Craig Breslow could pursue. One of them is a potential boom-or-bust candidate: Japanese slugger Teruaki Sato, who is seeking a move to MLB through the posting system.
Here's what to know about Sato, a triple-crown winner in Japan's Central League, and why he could be a fit in Boston.
MORE: Inside Payton Tolle's breakout 2026 season
Will Teruaki Sato Be Posted to MLB?
Sato, who plays for the Hanshin Tigers of the Central League in Japan, has been seeking a move to MLB this offseason. As of Monday, his Tigers squad made it official, announcing that Sato would be posted to MLB teams this offseason, per MLB Trade Rumors.
He won the Triple Crown in the Central League, also claiming MVP honors, making him a fascinating potential addition for an MLB franchise this offseason. "At least five" teams have already shown interest in Sato, per MLB Trade Rumors, and in a weaker offensive free-agent class, he could be one of the top available bats.
Sato, 27, is still relatively young and can play third base or right field. It's his bat, however, that would be an asset, as he's been one of the best hitters in Nippon Professional Baseball over the last two seasons. In 2026, he had a .306/.383/.609 slash line with 39 homers and 106 RBI, winning the Triple Crown.

Sato wouldn't officially be posted "until some time after the NPB season is over," per MLB Trade Rumors. He would have 45 days to sign with an MLB team after being posted, a timeline that could be impacted by a potential lockout — if he didn't have a contract by Dec. 1, his timeline would pick up where it left off after a lockout ends. If Sato didn't have a contract by the end of the 45-day period, he would return to the Central League in 2027.
After also playing for Japan in the 2026 World Baseball Classic, Sato could join the likes of Shohei Ohtani, Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Seiya Suzuki, Shota Imanga, Roki Sasaki, Munetaka Murakami, Kazuma Okamoto and more Japanese stars to join MLB in recent years.
Why Red Sox Could Be A Fit for Teruaki Sato
It's no guarantee that Sato will decide to join MLB, but it appears more likely than not that he'll land a free-agent deal this offseason, especially considering the thin market for bats. Considering Boston has a clear need for a slugger, it wouldn't be surprising to see Breslow kick the tires on adding Sato.
Under Breslow, the Red Sox have proven willing to pursue top Japan talent, signing Masataka Yoshida to a five-year deal in 2023. That deal has not panned out as anticipated, with Yoshida hitting 34 home runs over four seasons, but perhaps Breslow views Sato differently as a final piece to Boston's lineup, needing some power.
In a best-case scenario, Murakami is an example for teams to be encouraged about when considering Sato, a high-strikeout slugger from Japan coming to MLB. After signing with the White Sox last offseason, Murakami hit 35 home runs on a resurgent Chicago team that returned to the postseason, although he also hit .207 with 196 strikeouts.
With Jarren Duran facing an uncertain future in Boston, it wouldn't be surprising to see the Red Sox pursue a slugger — either at DH or in the outfield — to pair with Ceddanne Rafaela, Wilyer Abreu and Roman Anthony. Sato would also be capable of playing third base, where Curtis Mead is currently projected to start in 2027.
He may not be a seamless fit, and the strikeout issues could be a red flag, but there's reason to believe Sato could succeed in Boston. At the very least, he's one of few power bats who could be available, something the Red Sox need.

item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox could add more than one power bat by putting Seiya Suzuki on their offseason shopping list.
They could also make their lineup more flexible, provided they settle the playing-time questions before committing.
Boston.com’s Conor Ryan identified Suzuki as a potential fit earlier this month. The argument is worth revisiting as the free-agent market approaches, though it doesn’t mean Boston has opened negotiations.
Suzuki finished 2026 with a .270/.368/.473 slash line and 26 home runs, according to Baseball Savant. Those numbers supply the obvious attraction. His ability to work in an outfield and designated hitter rotation creates the more interesting question for Boston.
Suzuki Could Add More Than Right-Handed Power
FanGraphs’ playing-time record lists 111 games in right field and 30 at designated hitter this season. Boston would therefore be evaluating someone with recent experience in both roles.
That flexibility could matter when building a schedule around Roman Anthony. If the Red Sox want Anthony to play DH occasionally, an acquisition who can play the outfield offers more options than a hitter restricted to one lineup spot.
It wouldn’t create extra plate appearances on its own. Boston would still have to account for Wilyer Abreu and the rest of its outfield, and any arrangement would depend on how the roster changes.
The point is to evaluate Suzuki as part of a full alignment. A lineup that gets stronger on days Anthony needs a different assignment has value beyond one player’s home run total.
That is also why an apparent outfield surplus can be misleading. A group can look crowded on paper while still leaving the manager short of suitable choices when an injury or a planned rest day changes the preferred starting lineup.
That benefit would depend on defensive performance, health, and a role Suzuki would actually accept.
The Best Fit Still Needs a Realistic Price
Seiya Suzuki #27 of the Chicago Cubs warms up before game two of the National League Wild Card Series against the San Diego Padres at Petco Park on September 30, 2026 in San Diego, California. (Photo by Orlando Ramirez/Getty Images)
There are reasons to proceed carefully.
Suzuki is 32, so contract length would matter. Boston would need to consider how the proposed arrangement might change if more of his future playing time shifts toward designated hitter.
A flexible player can become a less flexible investment if the contract outlasts the skills that made the original fit attractive. That possibility belongs in the evaluation alongside his offensive production.
The Red Sox should also avoid assuming Fenway Park would automatically produce a career season. A favorable theoretical fit still has to survive the opposing pitchers, daily workload, and normal variation of a long schedule.
A signing would work best if it improved Boston’s choices throughout the week, rather than forcing the same difficult compromise into every game.
Suzuki deserves consideration because Boston can imagine a specific job for him beyond simply adding a recognizable name. The decision should follow a clear plan: identify the available at-bats, establish a realistic defensive workload, and decide what that combined role is worth before entering a bidding contest.

item.content:encoded:
Sooner or later, the Chicago Cubs will have to address the many question marks heading into the offseason, with one of the biggest concerns surrounding their outfield.
With both Ian Happ and Seiya Suzuki potentially heading to the open market, the Cubs could suddenly find themselves down two corner outfielders. If that happens, they will need to do whatever it takes to fill those spots with reliable players.
The Cubs' goal will be to retain at least one of those two players, but given how active the free-agent market could be, that may not be as easy as it seems. If the Cubs can't bring one of them back, don't be surprised if they look elsewhere. Randy Arozarena could be an option in left field and, at the very least, could help fill one of those two spots.
Despite being 32, Arozarena still has plenty left in the tank. Given the way he plays the game, especially defensively, adding that kind of energy alongside Pete Crow-Armstrong could be a great fit. Comparable to Suzuki in terms of age and offensive production, Arozarena is coming off an impressive season and has established himself as an above-average hitter since becoming an everyday player with the Tampa Bay Rays.
This past season proves it: Arozarena slashed .281/.381/.484 with a 151 wRC+. He added 26 home runs while posting a 10% walk rate and a strikeout rate just above 20%. Those numbers reflect a disciplined approach at the plate and help explain why he remains a productive offensive player.
As impressive as his production has been, concerns about Arozarena are growing. His overall bat speed and barrel rate are trending downward, raising questions about whether he can sustain his recent success. Still, this year's free-agent class offers few proven, productive bats, making a player with Arozarena's offensive capabilities hard to overlook.
Another major concern is his defensive value, as he continues to grade out near the bottom of the league. For a team that prides itself on defense and making plays for its pitchers, would adding a below-average defender in left field to replace a potential Gold Glove-caliber outfielder really make sense?
Maybe not. Still, the Cubs need to find ways to improve their roster, and Arozarena could offer an offensive upgrade in left field. What he may lack defensively, he could make up for with his postseason experience. On the biggest stage, Arozarena has built a reputation as one of baseball's most dangerous postseason performers.
Known for delivering in big moments, Arozarena could bring a spark to a Cubs team that has struggled to create memorable postseason moments in recent years. That kind of energy and experience could provide something the franchise hasn't enjoyed consistently since its 2016 championship run.
Another aspect of Arozarena's game that is sometimes overlooked is his ability on the basepaths. He added 23 stolen bases to his 26 home runs and impressive offensive numbers, giving him another dimension that could benefit the Cubs.
His speed would pair nicely with what Crow-Armstrong brings to the table, potentially giving the Cubs another base-stealing threat near the top of their lineup. With career highs in batting average, on-base percentage, and slugging percentage, Arozarena is coming off one of the best offensive seasons of his career.
Producing at that level at this stage of his career is somewhat surprising, but it also raises an important question: Can he do it again?
Some players take longer to find their footing in the big leagues, and Arozarena's career has followed a somewhat unconventional path. He didn't receive a regular, everyday opportunity until he broke through with Tampa Bay. Since then, his production has had its ups and downs, including during his time with the Seattle Mariners.
Even so, Arozarena has shown that he can be a productive offensive player, and his recent success in Seattle has only added to the intrigue surrounding his free agency. The question now is whether the player we saw this past season is the version of Arozarena fans can expect going forward or whether his production will regress toward his previous levels.
Arozarena is expected to command a lucrative contract, potentially worth at least $100 million, which could put him outside the Cubs' price range. However, given the team's potential outfield needs, don't be surprised if Chicago makes a serious run at him in free agency.

退団は不可避なのか…。今季限りでカブスとの５年契約が満了となる鈴木誠也外野手（３２）の去就が毎日のように米メディアでクローズアップされている。
１９日（日本時間２０日）には、今オフＦＡとなる選手に今季の所属球団が提示できる１年契約「クオリファイング・オファー（ＱＯ）」の規定額が「２３１５万ドル（約３６億円）」になったと伝えられた。攻守にわたる活躍でカブスの主軸となっている鈴木もＱＯを提示される可能性が十分あるが、残留には早くも絶望感が漂っている。
球団の専門メディア「ＣＵＢＢＩＥＳ ＣＲＩＢ」は「昨年、ＦＡ選手の１人がこのオファーを受け入れたが、鈴木の場合はそうならない可能性が高い」と断じた。というのも、鈴木は４年連続で２０本塁打以上と安定した長打力を発揮するだけでなく、ゴールドグラブ賞では右翼手部門の最終候補にも残っている。
同メディアはブルージェイズをはじめ、マリナーズやヤンキースなどが獲得に乗り出すとみられることを伝えた上で「ＱＯの有無にかかわらず、入札合戦が繰り広げられる可能性が高い。それがカブスが再びチームに迎え入れられない主な理由」と諦めモードだ。
鈴木の新契約は１億ドル（約１５８億円）規模になるとも試算されている。カブスも資金注入に本腰を入れれば引き留められる可能性もあるが、同メディアは悲観的だ。
「確かに今オフシーズンに１億ドル以上の年俸負担が軽減されるカブスには、鈴木の争奪戦でトップに立つだけの資金力がある。しかし、資金の大部分が投手陣の補強に充てられる見込みで、カブスが鈴木の争奪戦に勝つことを事実上不可能にしている」
鈴木を残したくてもすべてを残留費用に回すわけにもいかない。「ＱＯを提示する可能性はあるが、結末は既定路線」と流出は避けられないとみられている。

item.content:encoded:
When the 2026 Major League Baseball season officially comes to an end, the next big thing to watch is going to be what happens with two-time Cy Young Award winner Tarik Skubal.
Skubal is the biggest free agent prize of the year, without a doubt. He follows in the footsteps of guys like Shohei Ohtani, Juan Soto and Kyle Tucker, who were the biggest free agents of the year over the last three years. This year, it's time for Skubal to cash in.
Beyond Skubal, the biggest free agents of the offseason are Randy Arozarena, Seiya Suzuki, Robbie Ray, Shota Imanaga and potentially Bo Bichette. Bichette has an opt-out in his deal with the New York Mets. It's going to be a fun few months across the league. Let's try our hand at projecting what it could cost to sign these top names.
Tarik Skubal — Starting Pitcher
Skubal's stint in free agency is going to be fascinating. On one hand, you have the hurler who has been the most dominant starter in baseball over the last three years, at least. On the other hand, Skubal is heading to free agency at 29 years old and after undergoing elbow surgery earlier in the season.
Skubal is the best player heading to the open market and he will get paid well. He even could get paid historically well. ESPN's Jeff Passan shared in a column that if there is no salary cap, he could double the $245 million deal Stephen Strasburg got from the Washington Nationals, at most. Arguably, that is far too high. Yoshinobu Yamamoto has the largest contract for a starter in big league history at $325 million over 12 years, but he got that at 25 years old. Gerrit Cole is a closer equivalent. He got his nine-year, $324 million deal at 29 years old. Skubal should come in much closer to that from a years perspective. But could very well top Yamamoto's overall value.
Projection: 8-years, $335 million ($41.8 AAV).
Randy Arozarena — Outfielder
Arozarena is a three-time All-Star, including each of the last two years, and is coming off a 5.7 WAR season. He picked a good time to have one of the best seasons of his career. Arozarena is the best non-Bichette bat heading to the open market, which should do wonders for his value.
Projection: 5-years, $120 million
Seiya Suzuki — Outfielder
Suzuki is the second-best non-Bichette offensive player heading to the open market. He's coming off a season in which he hit 26 home runs, drove in 86 runs and logged 31 doubles in 143 games played. He'll be 32 years old when the 2027 season begins. He should do quite well this winter.
Projection: 4-years, $90 million
Robbie Ray — Starting Pitcher
Ray may be 35 years old, but he can still get it down. He had a 3.59 ERA in 31 total appearances in 2026, including 30 starts, with the San Francisco Giants and the San Diego Padres. He was an All-Star in 2025. Ray won't turn 36 years old until October, 2027. He should get one more multi-year deal this offseason.
Projection: 3-years, $55 million
Shota Imanaga — Starting Pitcher
Imanaga is just 33 years old and hasn't had more than a 3.77 season ERA in his three-year big league career. He's younger than Ray and has been arguably better over the last three seasons. He should do even better in free agency.
Projection: 3-years, $64 million
Bo Bichette — Infielder
Bichette is going to be among the most intriguing players to follow over the next few weeks. Skubal is clearly the best free agent heading to the open market. If Bichette opts out, he'll be the second-best. Bichette is owed $42 million from the Mets, if he sticks around in 2027. Then, he has a $42 million player option for 2028.
It's hard to believe, but Bichette is still just 28 years old. If he were to enter the open market again, there should be a massive deal with his name on it.
Projection: 6-Years, $200 million

item.content:encoded:
The upcoming free agent market is going to be thin, to say the least.
Right now, the top offensive weapons scheduled to head to the open market are outfielders Randy Arozarena and Seiya Suzuki. Arozarena smacked 26 home runs and drove in 79 runs in 54 games for the Seattle Mariners in 2026. Suzuki hit 26 home runs and drove in 86 runs for the Chicago Cubs in 143 games played. Outside of these two, the top offensive bats who are pending free agents are George Springer, Gleyber Torres, Trent Grisham, Ian Happ, Eugenio Suarez, Jonathan India, among others. There's a clear difference between Arozarena and Suzuki, and the rest of the top bats heading to the open market.
One guy who could throw a wrench into free agency is infielder Bo Bichette. The two-time All-Star has an opt-out to consider this offseason. If he doesn't use it, he'll make $42 million in 2027. If he does use it, all of a sudden he becomes the most intriguing offensive free agent. Plus, it helps that the third base market is going to be very thin.
What Should Bo Bichette Do?
Bichette didn't have a great 2026 season. He slashed .260/.312/.390 with 18 home runs and 78 RBIs in 160 games played. But he is still just 28 years old. He'll turn 29 years old before the 2027 season begins. Both Arozarena and Suzuki will be 32 years old by the time the 2027 season starts. Bichette is roughly four years younger.
When it comes to third base specifically, Suarez technically has a mutual option, but those are rarely ever picked up. Suarez is now 35 years old and batted .212 in 2026. He has significant pop, but didn't make contact and isn't great defensively at this point. Alec Bohm will be a free agent. He's 30 years old and has question marks himself. After Bichette, Suarez and Bohm, the next best options will be guys like Isiah Kiner-Falefa, Yoan Moncada and Jeimer Candelario.
If Bichette becomes available, he is head and shoulders above the rest of the potential third base free agent options. Plus, he can play other spots in the infield as well. Bichette was the Toronto Blue Jays' shortstop for years and he can play second base as well.
At the end of the day, Bichette has a decision to make. If he opts out, he should be in line for an even bigger multi-year deal.

カブス・鈴木誠也外野手（３２）の市場価値が高騰中だ。今季限りで５年契約が満了となり、来季の所属球団がどこになるのか米メディアを連日にぎわせている。

item.content:encoded:
MLB free agency takes on a new urgency this winter with a Dec. 1 lockout on the horizon. That could change how teams operate — and, eventually, how much money teams are allowed to spend, or even forced to spend. There are a ton of unknown variables at this point.
What we do know (for the most part) are which stars will be available to sign when the market does open up. From Los Angeles Dodgers ace Tarik Skubal to top Japanese free agent Teruaki Sato, here are the 10 best free agents (according to FanSided's Robert Murray) with projected contracts and destinations.
LHP Tarik Skubal
Projected deal: 9 years, $378 million ($42 million AAV) with New York Mets
Regardless of how CBA negotiations shake out, Tarik Skubal's long-rumored $400 million price tag may ultimately prove to be an overestimation. There's a reason no pitcher has ever received such a paycheck, Shohei Ohtani notwithstanding. Still, Skubal should become the highest-paid pitcher in MLB history. His durability, both in-game and season-long, combined with razor-sharp stuff in the prime of his career, should give teams the confidence to invest in Skubal over an extended period.
The Dodgers are the natural landing spot after acquiring him at the trade deadline, but the Mets are baseball's richest team and there's mounting pressure for New York to start competing, in a serious way, with Juan Soto and Francisco Lindor. Skubal is the ultimate floor-raiser in a rotation, and he'd form a mean one-two punch with breakout ace Nolan McLean.
OF Seiya Suzuki
Projected deal: 4 years, $100 million ($25 million AAV) with Toronto Blue Jays
Seiya Suzuki is probably the best bat available in free agency. The 32-year-old outfielder has been a model of consistency for the Cubs, with at least 20 home runs and an .800-plus OPS in three straight seasons. He's a plus defender in right field, too, where he posted career-best metrics in 2026. Suzuki has a rocket-like arm and consistently holds runners from the back corner.
Plenty of teams will take an interest in Suzuki's right-handed power profile; he draws walks and operates with sage discipline in the batter's box, despite occasionally elevated strikeout numbers. In the end, Toronto represents the most logical intersection of need and financial firepower to outbid the field.
OF Randy Arozarena
Projected deal: 5 years, $110 million ($22 million AAV) with Philadelphia Phillies
Randy Arozarena set new career highs in average (.281), OPS (.865) and home runs (26) in his walk year, emerging as one of the few bright spots on an otherwise disappointing Mariners team. He's more adequate than exceptional with his glove, but Arozarena provides middle-order power and he's a great personality hire.
The Phillies need Arozarena's bat and competitive fire in equal measure, plus he can help to safely return Bryce Harper to first base next season. Philadelphia desperately needs a right-handed slugger behind Harper in the lineup; the ability to finally add some stability to the outfield depth chart, as opposed to a 2026 rewind of the Adolis García or Max Kepler situations, should greatly appeal to a desperate Dave Dombrowski.
3B Teruaki Sato
Projected deal: 3 years, $75 million ($25 million AAV) with New York Yankees
Teruaki Sato is the most accomplished international free agent hoping to come Stateside this offseason. An MVP candidate in Japan's NPB, Sato hit .306 this year with 39 home runs and a .991 OPS. There are swing-and-miss and defense concerns, not dissimilar to the vague uncertainties that tanked Munetaka Murakami's stock last winter. Murakami ended up on a two-year deal with the White Sox, which he immediately outperformed.
Sato's left-handed power and upside at 27 years old could mean his market flourishes. But, given the baked-in gambles that come with signing an international free agent, he could end up getting lowballed, much like Murakami. A three-year, $75 million contract gives Sato a nice payday upfront while still hedging against potential struggles with a short-term framework. The Yankees need an infield slugger and have the money to roll the dice, so to speak, on Sato's immense talent.
LHP Trevor Rogers
Projected deal: 3 years, $60 million ($20 million) with Baltimore Orioles
Trevor Rogers has dealt with his share of injuries and inconsistency over the years, but he's coming off of two strong campaigns in Baltimore — and he's only 28 years old, so there's room left to establish himself as more than a third or fourth starter type. He couldn't recapture the success of 2025, when Rogers returned from injury to post a 1.81 ERA in 18 starts, but his 4.03 ERA last season does not capture the strength of his stuff (3.60 xERA). Moreover, the career-high 30 starts and 169.2 innings pitched was a nice addition to his résumé.
Teams will probably balk at dropping a full bag on Rogers' doorstep, ultimately, which opens the door for a short-term contract (probably with an opt-out clause or two) and a return to Baltimore. The Orioles need pitching badly and there are precious few better options than Rogers floating around the open market. This contract could turn into a total bargain.
RHP Freddy Peralta
Projected deal: 4 years, $84 million ($21 million AAV) with Chicago Cubs
Freddy Peralta's walk year has been a roller coaster of emotions. He bombed in New York after the Mets dealt multiple top-100 prospects to acquire him in an offseason trade. Then, after relocating to Tampa at the trade deadline, Peralta started slow before gradually picking up steam in September. Down the stretch and into the playoffs, he has looked more like the Cy Young candidate we witnessed in Milwaukee last season.
Peralta has not made the strongest case to prospective suitors in 2026, so a one-year, high-AAV deal to "prove it" is on the table. Ultimately, however, the 30-year-old should still be able to coax a substantial multi-year offer out of a desperate contender. His longtime NL Central rivals, the Cubs, are one such desperate contender. Peralta could join with the now-healthy Cade Horton and Justin Steele to revitalize Chicago's World Series hopes for 2027.
C Ryan Jeffers
Projected deal: 4 years, $68 million ($17 million AAV) with Minnesota Twins
The catcher market is tough to project, as there are so few who can hit like Ryan Jeffers. He was excellent in Minnesota this season, with 14 home runs and an .814 OPS in roughly half a season. He's the best catcher on the market, but Jeffers is not exactly lauded for his defense nor his game management behind the plate. He is not without injury concerns either, while even the best catchers end up in a timeshare eventually (especially when, like Jeffers, their glovework can be problematic).
Since there is such an absence of reliable hitters at the catcher position, Jeffers should be able to land a solid multi-year deal in the middle of his prime. A return to the Twins should not be discounted, even with Eduardo Tait and Vahn Lackey coming up through the Minors on accelerated timelines. Minnesota made a conscious decision not to trade him at the deadline, after all. The Twins would probably like to compete next season.
RHP Michael King
Projected deal: five years, $120 million ($24 million AAV) with San Diego Padres
Michael King returned to San Diego last winter on a backloaded three-year deal with opt outs. After an excellent showing in the playoffs, he will probably axe the remaining two years and $66 million on that contract in hopes of securing more guaranteed money this winter. King is not the sexiest name on the pitching market by any stretch, but he has made himself into a dependable workhorse with October equity.
The Padres clearly love King and new ownership, with their stated intention to build a contender, will probably consent to a reworked contract. San Diego has a paper-thin rotation as is. Losing King without a viable alternative in place could be disastrous, as the Padres don't have the trade ammo to compensate for a free agency exodus.
2B Brandon Lowe
Projected deal: 3 years, $66 million ($22 million AAV) with Pittsburgh Pirates
Brandon Lowe arrived in Pittsburgh via offseason trade and immediately became the most bankable presence in their lineup, with 35 home runs, 96 RBI and an .824 OPS. The 32-year-old can get in trouble with swing-and-miss, but he's a slugging outlier at second base. Moreover, Lowe quietly posted some of the best defensive metrics in MLB last season after struggling for years on the defensive end. It's fair to be skeptical about Lowe's ability to sustain this elite defense into his mid-30s, but he did everything he could to maximize his value as a free agent.
To that point, it's hard to imagine the Pirates letting Lowe walk without a fight. Pittsburgh threw more money around last offseason, with the front office clearly committed to changing their postseason fortunes. It did not come together in 2026, but Pittsburgh has a dangerous lineup and a very talented pitching staff. There's potential for a breakthrough in 2027, especially if Lowe sticks around.
LHP Adrián Morejón
Projected deal: 4 years, $68 million ($17 million AAV) with Toronto Blue Jays
Adrián Morejón's mystery-shrouded absence in San Diego's NLDS loss to Milwaukee was a tough pill to swallow, but once again, the Padres end the season feeling like the second-best team in the National League. They were able to at least put a scare into the Brewers where even the Dodgers could not. Part of the reason for San Diego's success this season, despite dramatic fluctuations from their lineup, was an elite bullpen. Morejón was only the setup man to Mason Miller, but the 27-year-old southpaw is still among the best relievers in baseball.
Over the past three seasons, Morejón has a 2.58 ERA with 248 strikeouts in 223.1 innings. It's hard to find a more steadfast high-leverage arm, especially one as young as Morejón. He could get some real length on his contract in a reliever-needy marketplace. The Blue Jays figure to be as aggressive as any team this offseason; Morejón setting up Louis Varland, with Tyler Rogers and Spencer Miles to cover other late-inning spots, is a tantalizing proposition.

カブスとの５年契約が今季限りで満了となる鈴木誠也外野手（３２）に熱視線だ。安定した打撃に加え、守備力の向上でヤンキースのアーロン・ジャッジ外野手（３４）に代わる右翼のレギュラー候補として期待されている。
今季の鈴木は１４３試合の出場で打率２割７分、２６本塁打、８６打点、ＯＰＳ０・８４１の好成績。４年連続で２０発超えを果たしただけでなく、１４日（日本時間１５日）に発表されたゴールドグラブ賞の右翼手部門で初めて最終候補に選出された。以前は守備に対するチーム内の評価を得られず、ＤＨ専任となる時期もあったことを考えれば大躍進だ。
こうした攻守にわたる活躍があるからこそ他球団も放ってはおかない。米老舗誌「スポーツ・イラストレイテッド」の電子版「ＯＮ ＳＩ」は、ヤンキースの外野手の補強候補の一人として鈴木の名前を挙げた。しかもメジャー屈指の強打者・ジャッジの〝後釜〟という位置づけだ。
同誌は今季の鈴木を「彼のすべてが結実した年だった」と絶賛した上で「ケガに悩まされたシーズンを経て、ジャッジは今後、必然的に指名打者（ＤＨ）としての役割に限定されるだろう。２０２６年の鈴木がどれほど素晴らしい活躍を見せたかを考えれば、ヤンキースがこの日本人強打者を獲得できれば、ジャッジが去った後の外野陣は極めて充実した布陣となるだろう」と占った。
今季のジャッジは４月に右肋骨を疲労骨折。長期離脱を経て復帰したものの、９月に今度は右ふくらはぎの筋損傷で離脱した。そしてポストシーズンでは戦列に戻れないまま、チームは地区シリーズで敗退。ジャッジ自身にとって出場が６６試合にとどまったのは１年目の２０１６年、新型コロナの影響でシーズンが短縮された２０年を除いて最も少なく、来季はＤＨに転向すべきとの論調が強まっている。
ジャッジがＤＨで打撃に専念する代わりに右翼に空く穴を鈴木が埋めるという算段だ。その場合、「スペンサー・ジョーンズとコディ・ベリンジャーが中堅手と左翼手を務めることになる」とし「トレード期限直前に獲得した２選手（ルイス・ガルシアとエリオト・ラモス）と、ジアンカルロ・スタントンの全員を放出することになるだろう」と大胆な動きが必要との見方も示した。
年々進化を続ける鈴木の需要は高まるばかりとなりそうだ。

『MLB.com』は現地10月14日（日本時間15日）付で、同賞の最終候補に選出された選手を紹介する記事を掲載。鈴木について、「2025年から2026年にかけて、スズキほど守備を大きく向上させた選手はほとんどいない」と評価している。
同記事では「メジャーリーグでの最初の4シーズンはいずれもFRV（フィールディング・ラン・バリュー）はマイナスだったが、32歳のベテランは、今季は+8を記録した」と、守備指標の大幅な改善を紹介。
さらに、「スズキのDRS（守備防御点）は+14を数え、これは全右翼手の中で2番目に高い数字である」と、数字を挙げて最終候補入りの根拠を示した。
一方、ベンジについては、「23歳のベンジは、卓越した守備を武器に、ナ・リーグの新人王候補として一躍脚光を浴びた」と紹介。さらに、「彼は10補殺以上を記録した7人の外野手の1人であり、送球による守備貢献度を示すスタットキャストの指標『Arm Value』では、メジャーリーグ全体でトップだった」と、その強肩を評価している。
また、同記事では「ベンジは送球速度の指標『Arm Strength』で96.6マイル（約155.5キロ）を記録し、MLB全体で5位にランクインしている」と、強肩を裏付ける数字も紹介。新人ながら優れた守備力を発揮し、ナ・リーグ右翼手部門の最終候補に選出されたベンジの特徴にスポットを当てている。
キャロルについては、「肩の強さは平均以下であるものの、驚異的な守備範囲の広さでそれを補っている」と特徴を説明。さらに、「持ち前の卓越したスピードを生かして広範囲をカバーし、OAA（平均的な野手と比較してどれだけ多くのアウトを奪ったかを表す指標）は+10を記録した」と伝えている。
このOAAはMLB全体の95パーセンタイル（上位5％）に相当する。また、同記事は「昨季『ゴールドグラブ賞』の最終候補にも選出されたキャロルが、OAAで2桁の数値を記録するのはこれで3年連続となる」と紹介し、守備範囲の広さを継続して示している点を評価した。

The New York Yankees once again failed to win the World Series this year after having high expectations.
After sweeping the Boston Red Sox in the AL Wild Card series, the Yankees got swept by the Tampa Bay Rays in the ALDS. Due to this, New York should be aiming to strengthen their roster this offseason.
One major need that the Yankees have heading into the offseason is another impactful power hitter. Because of this, they are now being urged to sign one of this year's top free agents from the Chicago Cubs.
New York Yankees Urged to Sign Cubs Star
Joe Najarian of SI.com urged the Yankees to sign Cubs star outfielder Seiya Suzuki this offseason in a recent article.
"But after his injury-plagued season, Judge will inevitably be limited to DH duties in the future. And given how good Suzuki was in 2026, the Yankees' post-Judge outfield would be in very good shape if they sign the Japanese slugger," Najarian wrote.
With the Yankees needing another star outfielder, it is understandable that they are being linked to him. He would certainly be a big addition to the Yankees' roster if signed. This is because he has shown throughout his career that he is a star.
Suzuki just had an impressive season with the Cubs, too. In 143 games in 2026, he recorded 26 home runs, 86 RBI, and a .270 batting average. This is after he had 32 home runs and 103 RBI in 2025 with Chicago. With numbers like these, he certainly would give New York's roster more pop if signed.
Should the Yankees Make This Move?
With Suzuki being a star, it would make a lot of sense for New York to sign Suzuki. Landing Suzuki would be massive for a Yankees club that wants to have better success in 2027. This is because he is a very impactful player when playing at his best and could thrive in New York.
Suzuki is exactly the kind of player that a contender like the Yankees should be adding, too. He has been consistently good at the plate and would simply make New York a more difficult team to go up against.
The Yankees will have a ton of competition to land Suzuki, though. This is because he is not only coming off a great season but is one of this year's top pending free agents. Thus, he will generate a lot of interest around the league. This will only heighten his value.
Although this is the case, it still makes sense for the Yankees to sign Suzuki. They need to win a World Series during the Judge era. Due to this, they are in a position to make a splash for Suzuki.

Brandon Valenzuela, el hermosillense finalista por el Guante de Oro de MLB en su año de novato: ¿contra quién compite?
El receptor sonorense de los Blue Jays de Toronto figura entre los tres mejores defensivos de su posición en la Liga Americana. Conoce a sus rivales y la lista completa de los 60 finalistas.
El beisbol mexicano tendrá representación en la disputa por el reconocimiento defensivo más importante de las Grandes Ligas. El receptor hermosillense Brandon Valenzuela, de los Blue Jays de Toronto, fue anunciado este miércoles 14 de octubre como uno de los finalistas al Guante de Oro 2026, después de destacar detrás del plato durante su primera temporada en MLB.
El sonorense, de 26 años, competirá por el reconocimiento al mejor receptor defensivo de la Liga Americana contra Dillon Dingler, de los Tigres de Detroit, y Austin Wells, de los Yankees de Nueva York.
La empresa Rawlings presentó a los 60 finalistas, distribuidos en 10 categorías por cada liga, incluyendo la posición de jugador utility. Los ganadores serán anunciados el próximo domingo 1 de noviembre.
¿Por qué Brandon Valenzuela fue nominado al Guante de Oro 2026?
La nominación del hermosillense representa uno de los logros más importantes de su joven trayectoria, especialmente porque llegó a las Grandes Ligas apenas el 5 de abril de 2026 y rápidamente logró establecerse como uno de los receptores defensivos más destacados.
Durante su temporada de novato, Valenzuela disputó 91 encuentros con Toronto y se ubicó entre los cinco mejores receptores de MLB en métricas defensivas avanzadas.
De acuerdo con Statcast y FanGraphs, sus números fueron los siguientes:
- +11 carreras de valor defensivo (Fielding Run Value), según Statcast.
- +13.6 en calificación defensiva, de acuerdo con FanGraphs.
- +8 carreras mediante el enmarcado de lanzamientos, una habilidad que ayuda a convertir pitcheos cercanos a la zona en strikes.
- +5 carreras por sus tiros a las bases, reflejando su capacidad para controlar los intentos de robo.
- 19 corredores retirados en intento de robo, con una efectividad aproximada del 30.2%.
- 1.88 segundos de tiempo promedio de tiro a segunda base, desde la recepción de la pelota hasta su llegada a la almohadilla.
El mexicano también aportó ofensivamente, al registrar un promedio de bateo de .222, nueve cuadrangulares y 23 carreras impulsadas.
Su rendimiento le permitió formar una destacada dupla de receptores mexicanos con Alejandro Kirk, otro de los jugadores de Toronto reconocidos por su capacidad defensiva.
¿Quiénes compiten contra Brandon Valenzuela por el Guante de Oro?
El camino del hermosillense hacia el premio no será sencillo, pues deberá superar a dos receptores con números defensivos sobresalientes.
- Dillon Dingler (Tigres de Detroit): Es el actual ganador del Guante de Oro de la Liga Americana. Terminó la temporada con +17 en valor defensivo y una calificación defensiva de +22.1, liderando ambas métricas entre los receptores.
- Austin Wells (Yankees de Nueva York): Destacó por su capacidad para recibir lanzamientos y bloquear pelotas en la tierra. Registró +10 carreras de valor defensivo durante 2026.
- Brandon Valenzuela (Blue Jays de Toronto): Se colocó entre los mejores receptores defensivos pese a disputar menos encuentros que varios de sus competidores.
Dingler buscará conquistar su segundo Guante de Oro consecutivo, mientras que Valenzuela y Wells aspiran a obtener el primero de sus carreras.
¿En qué equipo de la LMP juega Brandon Valenzuela?
Aunque Brandon Valenzuela es originario de Hermosillo, Sonora, actualmente sus derechos en la Liga Mexicana del Pacífico (LMP) pertenecen a los Águilas de Mexicali, organización que lo adquirió mediante un intercambio con los Naranjeros de Hermosillo.
El movimiento se hizo oficial el 17 de junio de 2025, cuando los Naranjeros enviaron al receptor sonorense a Mexicali a cambio del infielder Milán Tolentino, hijo del exbeisbolista naranjero José Tolentino. El acuerdo fue de carácter definitivo entre ambas organizaciones.
Antes de su salida, Valenzuela había tenido actividad con los Naranjeros durante la temporada 2024-25, en la que disputó 28 encuentros, conectó 21 imparables, incluidos ocho extrabases, produjo 10 carreras y terminó con un promedio de bateo de .259.
El cambio se concretó cuando el catcher todavía pertenecía a la organización de los Padres de San Diego en el beisbol estadounidense. Posteriormente, el 31 de julio de 2025, pasó a los Blue Jays de Toronto en otro intercambio, esta vez a nivel de Grandes Ligas, por el infielder Will Wagner.
¿Quiénes son todos los finalistas al Guante de Oro 2026 de la Liga Americana?
Además de Brandon Valenzuela, entre los candidatos de la Liga Americana aparecen figuras como Bobby Witt Jr., Vladimir Guerrero Jr., Jacob deGrom y Cody Bellinger.
| Posición | Finalistas |
|---|---|
| Lanzador | Tanner Bibee (Guardians), Jacob deGrom (Rangers), José Soriano (Blue Jays) |
| Receptor | Brandon Valenzuela (Blue Jays), Dillon Dingler (Tigres), Austin Wells (Yankees) |
| Primera base | Vladimir Guerrero Jr. (Blue Jays), Vinnie Pasquantino (Reales), Christian Walker (Astros) |

Los Blue Jays de Toronto encabezan la Liga Americana con cinco finalistas, incluyendo al hermosillense, Vladimir Guerrero Jr., Andrés Giménez, Nathan Lukes y José Soriano, quien también jugó para los Angelinos durante 2026.
¿Quiénes son todos los finalistas al Guante de Oro 2026 de la Liga Nacional?
En el Viejo Circuito, los Cachorros de Chicago también consiguieron cinco nominaciones, mientras que peloteros reconocidos como Chris Sale, Matt Olson, Dansby Swanson y Pete Crow-Armstrong buscarán sumar otro reconocimiento a sus trayectorias.

| Receptor | Freddy Fermín (Padres), Gabriel Moreno (Diamondbacks), Luis Torrens (Mets) |

| Jardinero izquierdo | Jackson Chourio (Cerveceros), Ian Happ (Cachorros), Daylen Lile (Nacionales) |

¿Cuándo se anunciarán los ganadores del Guante de Oro 2026 de MLB?
Los ganadores serán revelados el domingo 1 de noviembre de 2026, durante una edición especial de Baseball Tonight, transmitida por ESPN.
En las nueve posiciones tradicionales, los premios se determinan mediante dos componentes:
- 75%: Votación de los managers y entrenadores de Grandes Ligas, quienes no pueden seleccionar a jugadores de sus propios equipos.
- 25%: Índice Defensivo de la Sociedad para la Investigación del Beisbol Estadounidense (SABR), que utiliza estadísticas para evaluar el rendimiento defensivo.
La categoría de utility cuenta con una fórmula especializada desarrollada por Rawlings y SABR.
Posteriormente también se realizará la elección de los Guantes de Platino, que distinguen al mejor jugador defensivo de cada liga mediante una combinación de estadísticas y votaciones de los aficionados.
Para Brandon Valenzuela, la nominación representa una oportunidad de conquistar uno de los premios individuales más importantes de MLB en apenas su primera temporada, llevando el nombre de Hermosillo y Sonora a la élite defensiva del beisbol de Grandes Ligas.

Until the Braves make clear otherwise, it's safe to assume that Ronald Acuña Jr. and Michael Harris II will be back in the Braves' outfield next season.
However, the third outfield spot could use an upgrade. Mauricio Dubón and Mike Yastrzemski shared left field this season, but Dubón is a free agent, and Yastrzemski leaves much to be desired. Left field should be a focus in free agency, and Randy Arozarena could be a great fit.
Arozarena is a three-time All-Star and has been an All-Star in back-to-back seasons for the Seattle Mariners. This year, he hit 26 home runs and hit .281. He has 53 home runs since joining the Mariners and could be an everyday player for the Braves.
Arozarena, 31, is not going to get the same love from the Mariners as other teams on the open market. It goes against the Mariners' organizational philosophy to pay big for a player on the wrong side of 30. Outfield-needy teams could be willing to overpay for Arozarena, and the Mariners likely won't match it, knowing they have young players ready to replace him.
Arozarena crushed left-handed pitching this year, but his defense is not the best. Still, the Braves need offense badly. Their offense was a huge problem in the postseason, and Arozarena has already had postseason success in his career.
There are plenty of teams that could be looking for outfielders on the open market, including the Philadelphia Phillies. The Braves should be willing to overpay to ensure he doesn't land with one of their rivals. Arozarena and Seiya Suzuki are the top options in free agency among outfielders this year. The Braves need to ensure they get one of them, and Arozarena already has tons of experience in left field.

item.content:encoded:
The Philadelphia Phillies will look to improve a roster that once again dealt with injuries and shortcomings, leading to an early exit in the postseason.
The two corner outfield spots are key areas Dave Dombrowski, Preston Mattingly and the front office will need to focus on, along with the bullpen.
Left field has been a platoon over the last two seasons, while the team has struggled to get typical corner outfield production from a right fielder since Nick Castellanos’ All-Star season in 2023, where he clubbed 29 home runs and drove in a career-best 106 runs.
Since 2021, the Phillies have had 26 different starters in left field, with Brandon Marsh, Kyle Schwarber and Andrew McCutchen getting the majority of the starts during that stretch.
Over in right field, the Phillies also penciled in 26 different names to patrol right field, with Nick Castellanos and Bryce Harper earning the lion's share.
Despite the upcoming free agent pool being quite shallow, Randy Arozarena and Seiya Suzuki are a pair of outfielders on the market that the Phillies should target that could provide stability for multiple seasons.
Entering his age 32 season next year (assuming there is a season), Arozarena could be an intriguing pickup for the Phillies. He was named an All-Star with the Seattle Mariners after slashing .281/.381/.484 with an .865 OPS. He hit 26 home runs and drove in 79 runs.
He posted a 151 wRC+ and 5.7 WAR.
Stacking him up to the hitters in the Phillies’ lineup this season, he would have ranked within the top five in AVG, OBP, SLG, OPS, HR and RBIs.
Arozarena is coming off essentially a career year. His triple slash line numbers represent career highs in a full season for the outfielder, and it could have been an outlier campaign for him.
Nonetheless, even his career numbers at .255/.350/.442 and .792 OPS, along with his ability to hit 20-plus homers in six straight seasons, warrant a phone call from the Phillies, who may need him more than any other team in the league.
He would provide much-needed pop from the right side of the plate, something this lineup has been missing for a few years. This season, the Phillies ranked 22nd in MLB in OPS and 28th in on-base percentage from their right-handed hitters.
He also has more speed on the basepaths than Suzuki, adding some athleticism to a Phillies lineup that can become station-to-station at times.
Defensively, he isn't great, but the Phillies need stabilizing bats in the lineup due to the consistent ebbs and flows this lineup has endured over the course of the last handful of seasons, especially come playoff time.
Perhaps the biggest selling point for Arozerena may not be what he does over 162 games, but what he's already done when the stakes are highest.
His postseason résumé gives him an element Suzuki simply doesn't have at the major league level—a proven ability to become a difference-maker when the calendar flips to October.
Arozarena has plenty of experience playing in big moments. He has played in 45 career postseason games, slashing .292/.380/.565 with a .946 OPS across 184 plate appearances. He also has hit 12 bombs in the playoffs and has a knack for the theatrics.
Bringing him in would more than likely mean Brandon Marsh would be traded. The veteran is not a platoon-type bat and would be an everyday plug-and-play-type offensive piece in the middle of the lineup.
He won't be cheap.
Coming off one of his best seasons offensively, he will more than likely command a contract north of $100 million.
While not young either, the Phillies may not have a choice but to add another player in his 30s into the mix to capitalize on the closing title window.
Suzuki, who will turn 33 late next season, would bring similar traits to the lineup that Arozarena would, but perhaps on a more consistent level.
This season, he slashed .270/.368/.473 with an .841 OPS to go with 26 homers, 86 RBIs and a wRC+ of 134.
His 81 walks and 5.1 wins above replacement were career watermarks. It also marked a fourth consecutive season that he posted an OPS north of .800 and third in the last four years, where it was .840 or better.
The outfielder has been a consistent middle-of-the-order bat during his tenure with the Chicago Cubs.
Since 2023, he has had at least 140 hits, 27 doubles, 20 home runs and 70 RBIs. He would be two seasons removed from his best campaign of his five-year big league career in 2025, where he posted career-best in home runs (32) and RBIs (103).
His 113 career home runs are the third-most home runs in Cubs' history, only behind Kris Bryant (138) and Hall of Famer Ernie Banks (136).
During that same stretch he has averaged 28 homers and 97 RBIs per 162-game season. He also averages 72 walks per season during that span, and his patient approach would go a long way for a Phillies lineup that has repeatedly had chase issues, especially in the postseason when it’s become magnified.
Suzuki owns a slightly better career walk rate (10.9%) compared to Arozarena (9.8%).
He’s also a significantly better defender and made major improvements in that department this season. His 14 defensive runs saved this season were good for 17th-best among all outfielders, as opposed to Arozarena’s -2.
The other caveat with Suzuki is that he would be a different type of signing for the organization.
Philadelphia historically has not ventured into signing top Japanese talent, whether directly from Japan or even once they become assimilated stateside in MLB.
Of course, it’s not easy to break into such a market when there is no prior history. Add the fact that the Los Angeles Dodgers have established themselves as the premier destination for Japanese stars looking to take their talents to the top league in the world; it makes it all that more difficult.
The Phillies recently tried their luck with Koyo Aoyagi, a right-handed pitcher the team signed to a minor league contract before the 2025 season. Aoyagi posted a 7.22 ERA between Double-A and Triple-A and never made it to the big league club.
Other examples include Tadahito Iguchi, who they traded for in 2007 and So Taguchi, who they signed after spending six seasons with St. Louis. Neither was the caliber player Suzuki is and is not a success story that the team could use as a recruiting pitch to some of the top players, like star third baseman Teruaki Sato, who plays for the Hanshin Tigers of the Nippon Professional Baseball League.
General manager Preston Mattingly reportedly took a trip overseas to observe the 27-year-old who could be making his way over to the United States.
The Phillies also shouldn’t just sign Suzuki to say they signed a Japanese talent.
However, the talent is there and Suzuki would stabilize right field, a position that has become a revolving door over the last few seasons.
Like Arozarena, Suzuki would command a multi-year deal northwards of $100 million after he signed a five-year, $85 million deal with the Cubs.
But for a Phillies team that has spent years searching for stability in right field since Bryce Harper moved to first base, Suzuki wouldn't be simply another expensive bat. He'd be a proven middle-of-the-order hitter who gets on base, provides above-average defense, and has demonstrated the kind of year-to-year consistency the position has lacked.
Both players certainly fit the needs of the Phillies and wouldn't be a bad starting point to fix this roster.

今の鈴木誠也を見逃すのは「悪魔的な所業」 米誌が指摘する今オフのFA市場で期待される198億円超えの“価値”
今オフにキャリア初のFAとなる鈴木(C)Getty Images
カブスとの5年契約を全うした鈴木誠也が、今オフのMLBにおけるFA市場の“目玉”となる雰囲気が漂っている。
32歳となって迎える今オフにカブスとの5年総額8500万ドル（約100億3000万円=当時のレート）の契約が満了となる鈴木。広島時代を通じてキャリア初のFAイヤーとなった今季は、3月のWBCで右膝後十字じん帯軽度損傷による負傷者リスト入りで出遅れたが、最終的に143試合に出場。打率.270、4年連続20発となる26本塁打、86打点、出塁率.368、長打率.473、OPS.841と上々のスタッツを残した。
本人もFA交渉への想いは隠していない。現地時間9月30日に行われたパドレスとのワイルドカードシリーズに敗れ、無念のシーズン終了となった試合後、鈴木は地元局『Marquee Sports Network』などの取材に「僕はFAが初めてになる。どういう動きで、どういう話し合いで進んでいくかが全く想像つかない」と心境を吐露。その上で「どう進もうが、自分のやるべきことをやりたい」と前を向いた。

One thing that Boston Red Sox chief baseball officer Craig Breslow has shown multiple times since taking over the organization is that he's not afraid to make a splash in the trade market.
If you look at the Red Sox's 2026 roster, you'll notice a handful of guys were added by way of trade. Garrett Crochet, Sonny Gray, Erik Miller, Johan Oviedo, Adley Rutschman, Curtis Mead, Andruw Monasterio, Caleb Durbin, Eli White and Willson Contreras, among others. The trade market has been Boston's avenue of choice to improve and nothing should be ruled out this winter. Sure, Boston's farm system isn't as good as it was a few years ago, in large part due to the trades, as well as promotions to the big leagues. But there are still plenty of pieces that could be used to bring talent to town this winter.
Arguably, the perfect fit would be Bryce Harper of the Philadelphia Phillies. The Athletic's Ken Rosenthal and USA Today's Bob Nightengale both have insinuated that Harper could be floated by the Phillies this offseason as a potential trade chip, if he is willing to waive his no-trade clause. We already have made the case for why he would be a great fit for Boston. But what could an actual trade look like? Here's a mock trade both sides should consider.
Red Sox Receive: OF/1B Bryce Harper
Phillies Receive: OF Jarren Duran, INF/OF Kristian Campbell, SP Tanner Houck
It's important to note that this is a mock trade. It's far more difficult to actually get a deal done, rather than talking about the idea. When it comes to Harper, the most important variables are whether the Phillies actually would be interested in trading the two-time MVP and then whether he would even be willing to waive his no-trade clause. If the answer to both of those questions was, "yes." Then, you could proceed.
The Phillies notably had a shaky outfield in 2026, plus Adolis Garcia is heading to free agency. Duran had a tough 2026 season, but this is also a guy who had 9.0 wins above replacement in 2024 and 4.9 wins above replacement in 2025. There are reasons to believe that he could get back to that level. Campbell would be the jewel of the deal. He's just 24 years old and already has a long-term deal. He could play in the outfield, or replace Luis Arraez in the infield.
When it comes to Houck, he's someone who is healthy now and who was an All-Star in his last full season in 2024. He got hurt in 2025 and missed all of the 2026 season, except the regular season finale. Still, he could either help in the rotation, or in the bullpen. Houck was selected in the first round of the MLB Draft in 2017, when Dave Dombrowski was still Boston's president of baseball operations.
Again, the idea of a Harper deal is a pipe dream right now. If the Phillies shop him and he is willing to waive his no-trade clause, then this could be more realistic. But there are also finances involved. He has five years left on his deal and will make just over $27 million in 2027 and 2028. Then, he'll make just over $23 million in each of the final three seasons. Are the Red Sox willing to take on that type of money? It would be better than spending something similar on Randy Arozarena or Seiya Suzuki.

Alex Bregman has officially won the 2026 Rizzo Award, but the victory was far from a blowout. According to Bleed Cubbie Blue, the new third baseman finished with a score of +26, just a half point ahead of Pete Crow-Armstrong. This marks the closest finish in the entire 13-year history of the award. The race was so tight that fans could only guess the winner until the very end of the season.
The Numbers That Tell the Story
The final standings show a massive gap between the top performers and the rest of the roster. Bregman led all free agent signings with his +26 mark, proving he was the most impactful new addition. Per Bleed Cubbie Blue, Crow-Armstrong followed closely with +25.5 as the top returning player. Ben Brown sat at +13.5, while the legendary Ian Happ and Aaron Civale both finished with +10. The top ten list is packed with talent, but the battle for first place was a genuine nail-biter.
At the other end of the spectrum, the bottom of the list tells a different story about the team's struggles. Nico Hoerner finished with -18, while Dansby Swanson landed at -17. Seiya Suzuki also ended up at -17, joining the group of players who had a rough season. The data shows a clear divide between the heroes who carried the team and the goats who dragged it down. Even the best teams have players who simply cannot find their footing when it matters most.
Why the Playoffs Changed Everything
The regular season heroics did not translate into a deep playoff run for the Cubs. The team was swept by the Padres in the Wild Card series, ending the season with barely a whimper. Bleed Cubbie Blue noted that the Cubs looked completely overmatched over those two days.
Despite the loss, the regular season data suggests the team was built to hit home runs. For almost the whole year, the roster stayed close to the top of the home run leaders. However, the playoffs exposed a lack of pitching depth that the regular season stats could not hide. The Padres had a clear plan and executed it perfectly against Cubs starter Matthew Boyd. They swung early and often, recognizing strikes and punishing mistakes. The Cubs needed a pitcher who could go seven innings against a good offense, and they simply did not have one.
Bregman's regular season success stands as a bright spot in an otherwise painful year. His +26 score proves he was the right choice for the club, even if the playoffs did not go as planned. The question now is whether the team can build on this individual success or if the roster needs a complete overhaul. The numbers do not lie about who helped the most, but the final score of the season remains the same. The Cubs are back to square one.

It didn't take long for free agent rumors to start swirling.
The Chicago Cubs were just swept by the San Diego Padres in the National League Wild Card Round a few days ago, and free-agent rumors are already circling the baseball world.
It will no doubt be a busy offseason for the Cubs, who have plenty of players hitting free agency. Players like Kevin Gausman, Shota Imanaga, David Peterson, and Carson Kelly will all test the open market this winter.
However, the biggest question mark this offseason for the Cubs is what they plan to do with their outfield. Both Ian Happ and Seiya Suzuki are free agents at the conclusion of this year's World Series. That leaves the team in a potential rough spot.
The Cubs have to answer one of these questions ahead of free agency:
- Do we bring back both Happ and Suzuki and simply run it back with the same outfield core?
- Do we pay Happ and let Suzuki walk, since he will cost much less?
- Do we pay Suzuki big money and let Happ walk because Suzuki gives us the best chance to win?
The front office will obviously weigh all these options ahead of free agency. However, it seems as if the Cubs have already made somewhat of a decision about Suzuki's future with the organization.
Patrick Mooney of The Athletic reported that "it's unlikely that the Cubs will get into a bidding war for Suzuki's services, let alone win one."
Hearing that the Cubs won't enter a bidding war for Suzuki doesn't bode well for their chances of getting him back. Teams like the Dodgers, Blue Jays, and Yankees are better suited to get into a bidding war for the slugger than the North Siders.
Mitch Bannon of the Athletic already reported that the Blue Jays will pursue Suzuki this offseason. Given that Toronto isn't afraid to spend on big-time players (e.g., Dylan Cease last offseason), there's a strong chance that the outfielder doesn't re-sign with the Cubs.
Losing Suzuki in free agency would be a big loss for the North Siders. He has been one of the team's best power hitters since the Cubs signed him out of Japan in 2022. The Japanese slugger has 113 home runs over his five MLB seasons and has 58 home runs with 189 RBI combined over the past two years.
The Cubs would be losing that power bat at the top of their lineup if he goes to another team. Unfortunately, it's very possible he does leave.

The Chicago Cubs saw their season comes to an end Wednesday night when they were eliminated from the Wild Card round of the National League playoffs by the San Diego Padres. The Cubs lost the series in consecutive games after earning a spot in the postseason in the final days of the season.
While their time in the postseason was short-lived, the Cubs had multiple winning streaks in the early part of the season that allowed them to challenge the Milwaukee Brewers in the National League Central Division. However, the Cubs could not match Milwaukee's consistency throughout the year, and they finished 14 games behind the Brewers.
The Cubs will almost certainly have multiple changes to their roster when the 2027 season gets underway. The Cubs have multiple free agents, including outfielders Ian Happ and Seiya Suzuki as well as pitcher Shota Imanaga.

However, the Cubs are not likely to get involved in the bidding for the top free agent expected to be available. Tarik Skubal of the Dodgers is expected to receive the top contract offer ever made to a pitcher in MLB history.
Skubal was traded by the Detroit Tigers to the Dodgers this summer. Skubal is represented by top player agent Scott Boras, and Skubal is a two-time Cy Young Award winner.
While a number of teams may get involved in the bidding for Skubal, an insider with ties to the Cubs does not believe the team will make a significant bid for the dynamic 29-year-old left-handed pitcher.

The Chicago Cubs saw their season come to an abrupt conclusion Wednesday night when they lost their second consecutive game to the San Diego Padres in the Wild Card round of the National League playoffs.
"Looking back at the 5 years, I don't know if I was able to reach the expectations that people had (for me) or for myself."
Seiya Suzuki hit 113 home runs as a Cub in his first 5 MLB seasons, behind only Ernie Banks (136) and Kris Bryant (138). pic.twitter.com/rzxffiIVtX
Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)
— Marquee Sports Network (@WatchMarquee) October 1, 2026
The Cubs had a streaky regular season, often showing their dominance in the first half of the season with notable winning streaks, but they were unable to keep up with the Milwaukee Brewers in the NL Central. They finished in second place to the Brewers, a full 14.0 games behind Milwaukee. They didn't clinch their playoff spot until the final days of the regular season.
Chicago ended the year and entered the postseason as the No. 5 seed in the National League playoffs. They had to go on the road to play the Padres. That proved to be a big disadvantage, because the Padres were among the hottest teams in Major League Baseball as the postseason got underway.
There could be significant changes on the Cubs roster as the team prepares for the 2027 season. Ian Happ and Seiya Suzuki, two veteran mainstays in the Cubs lineup, will be free agents in 2027 and it seems quite likely that both will be with new teams when the upcoming season gets underway.
Happ spoke in the locker room and it sounded like he was saying goodbye to the organization. "All I can say is that I love being a Cub," Happ said, per the Marquee Sports Network. "I've loved my time. I've loved the place, the people, Wrigley Field, the fanbase. And it's been truly special. I don't think there's a better place in baseball to play."
Pitcher Shota Imanaga will also be a free agent in the offseason, and he may not figure in the team's pitching plans for the future.

item.content:encoded:
SAN DIEGO — Was it a successful season in Wrigleyville?
It’s hard — even with baseball’s highest scoring lineup, best defense and best player — to judge 2026 as anything but a failure for the Cubs.
They set championship-level expectations and World Series goals.
Bowing out of the postseason after two games, their offense muzzled and MVP center fielder Pete Crow-Armstrong a non-factor, before the calendar even flipped to October?
They didn’t come close.
“The goal is to win, and we didn’t play well enough to do that,” third baseman Alex Bregman said. “It’s time to look in the mirror and get better.
“I know myself and a lot of these guys will be thinking about it every day of the offseason and let it fuel us. Just not good enough. We need to get better. In all areas.
“It starts now for everybody in this organization. Assess the year and come back and be better next year, because it wasn’t good enough.”
In the wake of such disappointment, there’s one overarching question: How does this not happen again?
It’s been back-to-back years of this, the Cubs dispatched by the rival Brewers in the NLDS a year ago. That was described as fuel for their fire this season, but the embers didn’t even burn long enough for a rematch.
Craig Counsell, whom the Cubs poached from those Brewers, has two early postseason exits in three seasons at the helm, with two years left on the contract that made him the game’s highest-paid skipper.
“We lost,” Counsell said. “There’s a response to it that we get to choose, and we’ve got to improve. Everybody can point at themselves and say, ‘We’ve got to get a little bit better.’
“We’re going to have to wait to accomplish the thing we really want to accomplish. … We didn’t finish it this year, and you hope that this has to be part of the journey to the ultimate prize.”
With the investments made in Counsell, Bregman, Crow-Armstrong and more, the expectations are not going to change. The Cubs will head into next season thinking World Series, just like this year.
But at least at the moment, they have a lot of questions to answer about how they’re going to get there.
What will make the 2027 group better equipped than the 2026 one?
That’s what the offseason — likely to be halted by a lengthy work stoppage — will teach us.
This was a roller-coaster campaign, with high highs and low lows, a lot of pitching injuries and a final-week downturn that came at exactly the wrong time.
The thoughts on the minds of everyone inside the losing clubhouse Wednesday were of further blows this team is about to take, the players who aren’t going to return, the pending free agents who were such a part of this group and its plan to deliver on those championship-level expectations.
“We’ll talk about the baseball plenty,” second baseman Nico Hoerner said, “but when you get through a locker room with people that you’re really close with and people that aren’t guaranteed to come back here — and not seeing this thing through the way a lot of us envisioned and believed in — that’s the stuff that doesn’t sit right and hurts.”
Perhaps most important for Jed Hoyer’s front office, the Cubs might have to replace their entire starting rotation, with lefties Matthew Boyd, Shota Imanaga and David Peterson, plus righties Clay Holmes and Kevin Gausman, all set to hit free agency.
Righties Cade Horton, Edward Cabrera and Ben Brown, plus lefty Justin Steele, make for an intriguing group of possible replacements, but all are coming off injuries, a risky play.
Then there’s the corner outfielders.
Right fielder Seiya Suzuki has been an offensive force it will be tough for the Cubs to replace; he’s expected to be one of the best hitters on the market and land a big contract.
Left fielder Ian Happ is a franchise fixture whose potential departure had teammates crying Wednesday night.
“He embodies the Cubs more than anyone I know,” shortstop Dansby Swanson said through tears.
Sentimentality is a rare reason to spend for baseball front offices. Happ didn’t have the type of offensive season he consistently has throughout his career though still played excellent defense and hit for power.
“All I can say is that I love being a Cub,” Happ said. “I’ve loved my time. I’ve loved the place, the people, Wrigley Field, the fan base. And it’s been truly special. I don’t think there’s a better place in baseball to play.”
With decisions to make, how Hoyer crafts his roster – and how these Cubs respond to another bout of playoff disappointment – will answer that overarching question, the only question that matters:
How do the Cubs make sure this doesn’t happen again?

MILWAUKEE -- To the Twins, it looked like a fastball you could see out of the hand – and then it was past you. To the Rockies, it was a pitch that seemed to reach the plate before they could react. The Braves geared up for 100 mph, then found themselves chasing cutters and sliders.
The Cubs had faced Jacob Misiorowski more than most teams. Their manager still described a fastball at the top of the strike zone that “nobody can hit.” The Phillies came within one Kyle Schwarber swing of literally getting no hits in nine innings.
“You see some guys that throw 103 [mph], but you get a little bit more time. A guy like that, where he's almost dropping it in the catcher's mitt, man, it makes for a tough day,” Judge said in May, after Misiorowski struck out 11 and touched 103.6 mph in his first career start against the Yankees. “I was excited to get a chance to face him and see him for the first time.
“You know, I’ve seen a lot of his games and seen what he's done; it's impressive stuff, man. They've got a great, great, great young star over there.”
Across the league, opponents spent the season looking for an answer when Misiorowski was on the mound. They struggled, as he finished with a 1.80 ERA, 252 strikeouts, a 0.80 WHIP and a .157 opponents’ average, each the best mark in the Majors. He enters October as the clear favorite for the National League Cy Young Award. On Saturday, the Padres will get the next chance when Misiorowski starts Game 1 of the National League Division Series.
Ask the hitters who faced him what makes the assignment so difficult, and velocity is only the beginning.
“Marshy asked me after the game,” said Phillies star Bryce Harper in June, referring to teammate Brandon Marsh, “he's like, ‘That's probably the best guy I've ever faced.’ And he asked me who’s one of the best guys I've ever faced, and I said Matt Harvey. He had that extension heater, and he was one of the first guys that really rode that heater at the top of the zone. Obviously, 104 [mph] is a little bit different.”
That was after Misiorowski’s finest start of the season, a 15-strikeout, 27-batter, 95-pitch shutout in front of a spellbound crowd at American Family Field on June 12, the one-year anniversary of Misiorowski’s Major League debut.
Harper, perhaps with October in mind, saw a silver lining.
“I'm happy we were able to face him – and I'm not saying that in a good way or bad way, but I was just happy we were able to face him and see what that looked like,” he said.
The Twins had their own trouble in an Aug. 9 matchup, when Misiorowski reached 200 strikeouts faster than all but one pitcher in history. Misiorowski began that night by throwing 21 consecutive four-seam fastballs. Royce Lewis saw one at 103 mph in his first at-bat and called it one of the most difficult pitches he had ever faced.
Brooks Lee noticed how far Misiorowski’s 6-foot-7 frame carried him down the mound, and how his position on the first-base side of the rubber changed the angle. Even a hitter who recognized what was coming had little time to do anything about it.
“It comes out of his hand and you feel like you see it well, and then it’s by you,” Twins hitter Kody Clemens said. “Especially up in the zone.
“If he throws a fastball in the upper part of the zone, I feel like it’s damn near impossible to hit.”
Twins manager Derek Shelton pointed to the pitch’s movement near the top of the zone. Hitters had to judge whether it would be a ball or strike while trying to catch up to 100-plus mph. He called it “probably one of the most challenging at-bats in the game.”
“Honestly, we were scratching, clawing, trying to get to him in any way, shape or form,” Colorado outfielder Cole Carrigg said.
Misiorowski threw 66 pitches at 100 mph or harder that day, a single-game record in the pitch-tracking era. Rockies manager Warren Schaeffer saw more than a radar-gun reading.
“That’s a one-of-one fastball, 103 with all that extension,” Schaeffer said. “It’s hard to react to that. And he throws it all the time.”
Against Atlanta in August, the problem changed shape. Misiorowski threw six scoreless innings in a matchup with Chris Sale, a pitcher he grew up admiring. Sale left impressed by “probably the most impressive fastball I’ve ever seen.” Braves manager Walt Weiss explained what happened when hitters prepared for it.
“You’re gearing up for 100, and then you’re having to deal with cutters and sliders,” Weiss said. “It’s among the toughest at-bats.”
The Cubs’ Seiya Suzuki had offered a similar assessment after facing Misiorowski in June, on the night he fired a 105.5 mph fastball against Pete Crow-Armstrong to match the third-fastest pitch since tracking began in 2008.
“Everybody had good swings and good at-bats,” Suzuki said through interpreter Edwin Stanberry, “but overall, he just pitched better.”
The Cubs did find a way through on Sept. 2 at Wrigley Field, scoring five runs in the first two innings and chasing Misiorowski after four while snapping his streak of 25 consecutive outings allowing three or fewer earned runs. Alex Bregman homered on a slider low in the zone and added a two-run single on a 102 mph fastball. Beforehand, Cubs manager Craig Counsell had identified the opening: Get a pitch lower in the zone, because the high fastball was so hard to hit even when hitters expected it.
“When he executes, you’re in trouble,” Counsell said. “That’s generally how the great ones are.”
Six days later, the Cubs saw him again. Misiorowski opened by striking out Crow-Armstrong on a 103.7 mph fastball, reached 104.5 against Suzuki and allowed one run over 6 1/3 innings. Along the way, he threw his 1,000th pitch of the season at 100 mph or harder.
“That’s how I throw,” Misiorowski said afterward. “The guys on the other side expect that.”
They do. By now, hitters from New York to Philadelphia to Minnesota to Colorado to Atlanta to Chicago, and across the entire league, can describe the fastball, the angle and the pitches that follow.
The Padres will arrive with their own plan. Then someone will have to stand in the box and try to make it work. Nobody has consistently done that against the presumptive NL Cy Young winner in 2026.

SAN DIEGO -- The lights cut out, Korn’s “Blind” blared, the sellout Petco Park crowd rose to their feet roaring and Mason Miller seemingly spawned onto the mound for the start of the ninth inning. The game was over. The National League Wild Card Series was over.
But in reality, it had ended well before that.
This is exactly why Padres general manager A.J. Preller assembled the best and deepest bullpen in baseball, for nights like Wednesday.
“In the postseason, you’ve got to get a lot of great hitters out,” Preller said. “You’ve got to have a lot of answers in that bullpen.”
After starter Nick Pivetta departed in the fourth, Padres manager Craig Stammen fully unleashed his bullpen over the final 5 2/3 innings against the Cubs in Game 2. Bradgley Rodriguez, Jason Adam, Adrian Morejon and Miller proceeded to allow just three men to reach base and keep Chicago’s league-best offense scoreless to slam the door on a 4-1 victory and send the Padres to the NL Division Series for a best-of-five-series against the Brewers.
Michael King going seven scoreless innings in Game 1 and saving the key arms in the back end set the Padres up perfectly to lean on that group the following night. If the Padres got an early lead, Stammen wasn’t going to mess around with keeping Pivetta in longer than he needed to secure the series.
That’s exactly how things played out.
San Diego scored a pair of runs in the second before Pivetta -- who did his job in limiting the Cubs over 3 1/3 innings -- got the hook in the fourth after giving up an RBI single to Nico Hoerner. A one-run lead ballooned to three after Gavin Sheets’ pinch-hit homer in the bottom half of the inning. The ‘pen took care of the rest.
“Michael’s effort last night was phenomenal and that allows us to go out firing in the early part of the game today and get our best guys out there,” Miller said. “It puts us in a really confident position. We get a lead and we feel really good about it.”
Perhaps the most important aspect of the Padres’ performance in this series was shutting down the Cubs’ elite lineup, and specifically their top two hitters in Pete Crow-Armstrong and Alex Bregman. The former is coming off the seventh 40-40 season in baseball history and the latter posted a 1.010 OPS in the second half.
They collectively went 0-for-15 in the series with eight strikeouts.
It was quite the statement, but it’s exactly what the Padres have been doing all season. By innings, San Diego had the fourth-most used bullpen in the Majors (683 2/3) and it possessed the fifth-best ERA (3.53).
“It’s an incredible group, top to bottom,” Adam said. “It doesn’t matter the situation, it doesn’t matter the inning, everybody out there is ready to go at all times. Fourth inning, ninth inning, I don’t care who we put out there, I feel really confident the guy is getting the job done.”
Rodriguez was the first into the fray, the rookie right-hander who immediately became one of the best relief arms in the sport and has been dominant in high-leverage situations throughout the year. He played fireman in the fourth, escaping a bases-loaded jam to preserve Pivetta’s line before pitching a clean fifth that he capped with a strikeout of Seiya Suzuki on a changeup below the zone.
“We’ve always known that about Bradgley -- that his maturity level is beyond his years,” Padres pitching coach Ruben Niebla said. “He doesn’t rattle. He doesn’t get nervous. He trusts himself and is a confident guy. We’re able to put him in those situations very confidently, and he’s responded well to that.”
Adam got through a 1-2-3 sixth, then Morejon cruised through the seventh and eighth, allowing just one hit, a Tyrone Taylor single. Then the ball was handed to Miller, the most imposing reliever in the game, who struck out an insane 47.4% of the batters he faced this season and finished with a career-best 1.67 ERA and 38 saves.
He gave up a double to Hoerner but struck out a pair and got Carson Kelly to ground out to end it, sending the Padres to Milwaukee and the Cubs back home.
“It’s not about any individual, it’s about a group,” Miller said. “It’s about passing the ball to the next guy and getting us in the clubhouse with a win. I think it’s a lot of selfless guys down there.”
Now, the Padres get the top-seeded Brewers in the NLDS, another team with plenty of firepower in the bullpen. To defeat them, and anyone else standing in the Padres’ way this October, Wednesday will be the template.
And if it continues to pan out the way it did, that should scare the rest of the postseason field.
“We knew we had six innings we could cover,” Niebla said. “It worked out to perfection.”
