What a way to sweep the Red Sox out of the playoffs! The Yankees brushed aside their inferior opponents, winning the two games by a combined score of 18-2. Every facet of their game was clicking — plate discipline, slug, bat-to-ball, two-strike hitting, situational hitting, base running, defense, and of course, starting pitching. It’s a winning recipe that leaves them in good stead for the upcoming ALDS date with Tampa.
The Yankees weren’t the only team to eliminate their opponents from the postseason on Wednesday so let’s jump straight into the action!
AL Wild Card Series Game 2
Chicago White Sox 7, Houston Astros 3
(Chicago wins 2-0)
After just two games, I can’t think of any playoff participant who wants to face these White Sox. That is a sentence that no one could conceive of typing at the start of the season. Two seasons removed from suffering the most losses in MLB history and on the back of three straight losing campaigns, this upstart Chicago squad came out of nowhere to crash the postseason, starting with a two game sweep of the Astros in their own building.
They have done so by scoring early and often, the White Sox lineup a deep unit one-thru-nine with multiple ways to hurt you. They work deep counts, foul pitches off, draw walks, and can put the ball in play, but can also slug the ball out of the yard from almost any spot in the batting order. On Tuesday, they scored three unanswered runs in the first two innings to put the Astros on the back foot from the word go, and Wednesday continued the trend with the Southsiders hanging a four-spot before the home team had a chance to bat.
They had a 1-0 lead just five pitches into the game against Astros ace Hunter Brown, Sam Antonacci leading off with a double before Kyle Teel drove him home with a single. A fielding error by Nick Allen on a Miguel Vargas grounder put a pair on, and three straight singles by Andrew Benintendi, Tristan Peters, and Chase Meidroth plated three more runs with help from a Lucas Spence throwing error from center.
Credit to the Astros, they did not roll over after going down four in the first and slowly chipped into the White Sox lead. Jeremy Peña led off the bottom of the first with a booming home run that clattered off the left field wall just below the train tracks. Cam Smith hit one to almost exactly the same spot with two outs in the second. Jose Altuve narrowly snuck a solo shot into the Crawford Boxes to lead off the fourth and just like that, a 4-0 game had become a 4-3 thriller.
An inning later it looked like the Astros would pull of the improbable and complete the comeback. Smith was hit by a pitch, Peña singled, and Isaac Paredes walked to load the bases with two outs for Altuve. However, reliever Anthony Kay got Altuve to fly out to medium right field to strand all three ducks on the pond. That left the door open for the White Sox to swing the momentum back in their own favor and they did so immediately. Benintendi and Peters drew a pair of walks to open the sixth, prompting Joe Espada to call on Bryan Abreu out of the bullpen. Astros owner Jim Crane vetoed a trade of Abreu to the Twins in the final minutes of the deadline, and Abreu rewarded that faith by hanging a 3-1 slider to Meidroth, the second baseman crushing a three-run bomb to left to put the final nail in the Astros’ coffin.
After sweeping this rematch of the 2005 World Series, the White Sox advance to the ALDS where they will face the AL Central champion Guardians, first pitch of Game 1 scheduled for 1:00 p.m. ET on Saturday.
NL Wild Card Series Game 2
Philadelphia Phillies 4, Atlanta Braves 3
(Series tied 1-1)
The Phillies’ season was hanging by a thread until some late heroics by Kyle Schwarber, Bryce Harper, and Alec Bohm sent this thrilling series to a decisive Game 3. It was a pitchers’ duel early between two starters trending in opposite directions. Tyler Mahle entered his first career playoff start with a sub-two ERA after joining the Braves from the Giants at the deadline while Cristopher Sánchez posted an ERA above five in the month of September (though will still likely wrap up his second straight runner-up finish in NL Cy Young balloting).
The one thing the two starters do have in common is first inning struggles and that certainly played out in this game. Mahle allowed a leadoff double to Trea Turner and consecutive one-out singles by Bryce Harper and Alex Bohm to allow the Phillies to jump ahead, 1-0. However, Sánchez issued a leadoff walk to Ronald Acuña Jr., who promptly stole second and scored the tying run on a Matt Olson single.
Both starters settled in from there, trading zeroes for the next five innings, until things unraveled for Sánchez and his defense in the seventh. Sean Murphy worked a leadoff walk and Ha-Seong Kim reached on a bunt single to put a pair on with no outs. Drake Baldwin then clubbed what looked like a routine liner to right, but Harper misplayed it horrifically breaking in on the ball only to watch it sail over his glove and to the wall for what was ruled as an RBI double. Sánchez intentionally walked Ozzie Albies to load the bases, and Olson made him pay with a sac fly to double the Braves lead, 3-1.
What should have been a hammer blow to the Phillies morale did not play out as such. Schwarber immediately responded with a towering leadoff shot off lefty reliever Dylan Lee, and Harper atoned for his misplay by going back-to-back to retie the game, 3-3. That sent this game to extra innings, where the much-maligned Alec Bohm continued his redemption tour. Bohm was on the bubble of being non-tendered during the offseason, but the Phillies kept him around and drove in the first run of the series with an RBI double in the first inning of Game 1. The third baseman was the ultimate hero in this one, his opposite field solo homer off rookie Didier Fuentes in the 10th to keep the Phillies season alive and force a decisive Game 3.
San Diego Padres 4, Chicago Cubs 1
(San Diego wins 2-0)
This game featured surprisingly quick hooks of both starters as neither manager wanted to risk leaving their highest leverage relievers unused. One was certainly more deserved than the other, Kevin Gausman allowing three runs on five hits in 3.1 innings. The Cubs were desperate for starting pitching at the Trade Deadline and Gausman was supposed to be their big prize. However, he flopped after making the move from the Blue Jays, pitching to a 4.83 ERA in nine starts post-deadline, and his stinker tonight was the beginning of the end of the Cubs’ season. Nick Pivetta on the other hand held Chicago to a run on three hits and two walks with four strikeouts in 3.1 innings, but Craig Stammen seemed determined to play the matchups in this one.
Ty France got things started with a double to lead off the second, advancing to third on a Jackson Merrill single, who then stole second to put a pair in scoring position for Xander Bogaerts. The veteran shortstop opened the scoring with an RBI single, which brought Ethan Salas to the plate. The 20-year-old became the youngest catcher ever to appear in a playoff game, and in his first postseason PA, he lifted a sac fly to center to plate Merrill as the Padres’ second run.
The real story of this series has been the Cubs’ inability to score. They led MLB scoring 5.25 runs per game, spearheaded by shoo-in NL MVP Pete Crow-Armstrong and his MLB-leading 45 home runs (PCA would go 0-for-7 with four strikeouts in the series). They found themselves shut out through the first 12.1 innings of this series, finally breaking the seal in the fourth on a Seiya Suzuki single, Ian Happ walk, and Nico Hoerner RBI single. A Carson Kelly hit-by-pitch loaded the bases with two outs, but Dansby Swanson flew out to stand all three in place.
San Diego immediately punished them for failing to fully cash in on that scoring opportunity. Bogaerts reached on a one-out double, prompting Craig Counsell to call on Daniel Palencia in relief of Gausman. Palencia yanked a 101 mph fastball right into Sheets’ nitro zone down and in, and the lefty crushed it to right for a mammoth two-run blast.
It was all hands on deck from there from the Padres bullpen looking to protect their lead for the final five innings of the contest. They proved how terrifying a relief corps they’ve been all season, allowing just three base runners — a Michael Busch walk with two outs in the fifth, a Tyrone Taylor pinch-hit single with one out in the eighth, and a Hoerner one-out double off Mason Miller in the ninth — after the Cubs stranded the bases loaded to end the fourth.
San Diego advances to the NLDS where they will face the best team in baseball. It’s an unenviable position to come up against presumptive NL Cy Young Jacob Misiorowski and the 103-win Brewers. Game 1 of that series is scheduled for October 3rd with first pitch time contingent upon the result of Game 3 between Philly and Atlanta.

【MLB】鈴木誠也と今永昇太の絆 「今年の5月、6月よくなっていったところは、鈴木選手から…」 “打者目線”アドバイスで状況好転の事実明かす
日テレNEWS NNN / 2026年10月1日 18時19分
◇MLBナ・リーグ ワイルドカードシリーズ 第2戦パドレス 4-1 カブス(日本時間1日、ペトコ・パーク)
パドレスに連敗しポストシーズン敗退となったカブス。試合後に今永昇太投手が今季、苦戦するなかで、鈴木誠也選手のアドバイスで活路を見い出した事実があったことを明かしました。
ポストシーズン敗退が決定し、試合後にインタビューに応じた今永昇太投手。登板できず今季を終えてしまったことに悔しさをにじませるなか、3年間チームメートとして過ごした鈴木選手について話題が及びます。
今永投手はメジャー挑戦1年目から、鈴木選手の支えがあったと語り、さらに「本当にこれ冗談抜きで今年の5月、6月よくなっていったところは、鈴木選手からアドバイスをもらった、ここではちょっと言えないですけど、バッターからの目線でアドバイスをもらった部分が大きかったので、やっぱりこのメジャーの世界ってデータが主流とか今、言われていますけど、僕はずっとこの2年間、ピッチャーから見た一方通行のデータしか見ていなかったので、バッターから自分を見た時にどうなのかというのは、あまり参考にしなかったというか、そういうデータをもらったりもしなかったので、バッターがどうされたら嫌なのかというのを、そういうヒントを与えてくれた存在なので、ものすごく感謝していますね」と述べ、アドバイスをきっかけに状態が好転したことを明かしました。
さらにワイルドカードシリーズで戦ったパドレスには、松井裕樹投手とダルビッシュ有投手が所属し、試合前や試合中には交流があったことも言及。「体の調子はどうだという話をダルビッシュさんにしていただいて、会話できる時間は少なかったですけど、松井選手も試合前なので長い時間いると今から戦うわけなんで、それはしないようにしていましたけど、彼もそれを感じるでしょうし、お互いの近況だったりとか、お互い嫌なチーム同士だけど、がんばろねというそういう会話でした」と会話の内容を明かします。そして試合中は、ブルペンが隣同士で松井投手がすぐ近くにいた状況だったことも明かし、「すごい違和感はありましたけど、松井裕樹選手の登板も見れて、ピッチャーとしてすごい興味があるので、いろんな球種を駆使して、僕と同じ左ピッチャーで似たようなタイプですけど、数値とか全く違ったので、自分にも勉強になりました」と語る一幕がありました。

カブスが敗退し、鈴木誠也外野手（32）が契約最終年のシーズンを終えた。ワールドシリーズ終了後のこのオフシーズンにはメジャー移籍後初めてFAとなる。
試合後は、シカゴの専門テレビ局「マーキースポーツネットワーク」など現地メディアの囲み取材に応じた。一問一答は以下の通り。
◇ ◇ ◇
－敗退しシーズンを終えた
「負けるっていうのはやっぱり悔しいですし、まあ勝負の世界、スポーツの世界ですけど、非常に悔しいなっていう…。ここまでみんな戦ってきて、1年間、最後こういう形で終わるっていうのは、やっぱりうれしいことではないですし。最後は笑って終わりたかったですけど。この悔しさをしっかりまた来年につなげていけたらいいなと思います」
－シカゴでの5年間を振り返って
「いやもう、思い出を語り出したら3時間ぐらい話さないといけないんですけど、いいですか？ まあでも、やっぱり初めてアメリカに来たのもカブスがあって、ここに来られて。で、素晴らしいチームメートだったり、スタッフ、いろんな人がサポートしてくれたから、今ここでこうやってしっかり戦えてるっていうのもあるので。すごく思い出もたくさんありますし、もちろんファンの皆さんのあの声援だったり、リグリーフィールドで野球をやるこの素晴らしさっていうのを、改めてもう一回やりたかったですけど。すごくいい思い出にはなってますね」
－FAについて
「家族もシカゴが大好きですし、FAのことは今年、僕が初めてになるので、どういう動きでどう話が進んでいくのか、まったく想像できないので分からないんですけど、この球団に思い入れがあるっていうのは、あるので。どう進もうが、自分のやるべきことはしっかりやりたいなと思います」
－FA市場でもトップクラスだと思うが5年間で証明してきたことをどう感じる
「正直あんまり、期待に応えられたのかって言われると、もっともっとできたんじゃないかなっていうか、もっと自分に期待してた部分もあったんで。悔しさが残るシーズンがほとんどだったのかなっていう風には思いますし。良いときも悪いときも、こう応援してくれた皆さんもいるんで、常に頑張ろうっていう風には思ってましたけど。自分では、あんまりこう、満足できた5年間っていう感じではなかったですけど、最後こうやって守備がしっかり向上して、周囲のみんなに信頼してもらえたっていうのはすごくうれしかったですね」

According to Toronto Blue Jays president and CEO Mark Shapiro, the team plans to re-explore the Japanese market this offseason. The Blue Jays will also be sending a contingency plan to Japan in the offseason, and Shapiro plans to travel there as they look to bolster the lineup.
The Blue Jays have already been successful with recruiting Japanese star Kazuma Okamoto, who had a stellar rookie campaign this season with 33 home runs. On Sept. 8, he became the fifth Japanese-born player to hit 30 home runs, earning a noteworthy milestone achievement.
Signing Okamoto to a four-year, $60 million contract last offseason was a massive win. While the team's offense and power output took a significant step backward this season, Okamoto was the driving force behind the team's power. All things considered, his success has persuaded the team to continue to find more Japanese talent.
While the Blue Jays are targeting Seiya Suzuki from the Chicago Cubs as well, the team has also been eyeing two big Nippon Professional Baseball (NPB) stars who are expected to be on the market this winter and have already gained significant attention from MLB teams.
Mark Shapiro says the #BlueJays will send a contingency to Japan this offseason and he may travel there, too, as they look to expand their presence (both baseball and business).
He added that the Japanese market will obviously be something they explore again this winter.
Japanese slugger Teruaki Sato and right-handed pitcher Kaima Taira are two talents that would help enhance the Blue Jays' needs ahead of the 2027 season. Sato would provide the Blue Jays with an elite left-handed power bat who is coming off a dominant 37-home-run season with an explosive 1.012 OPS for the Hanshin Tigers.
With Taira, he is expected to be one of the top arms on the market alongside Tarik Skubal, who is an elite starter and reliever. But as a starter, he led all of NPB with a 1.36 ERA, serving as a commanding presence for the Saitama Seibu Lions.
The Blue Jays would benefit from adding his arm, as he would provide high-upside pitching depth to the rotation as well as a bullpen safety net. His versatility makes him an intriguing option to add as the team faced a heavily taxed pitching staff this season. While the Blue Jays are expected to get Cody Ponce, Bowden Francis and Jose Berrios back in 2027, you can never have enough pitching, and this past season proves it.

The MLB playoffs are in full swing, as Wild Card matchups began this week.
For the Los Angeles Dodgers, they are still awaiting their opponent for the NLDS. It will be either the Atlanta Braves or the Philadelphia Phillies.
Amid the MLB playoffs, the Dodgers made a few roster moves in preparation for their upcoming series.
More MLB on Heavy: Atlanta Braves Announce Tyler Mahle News After Dramatic Phillies Game
Los Angeles Dodgers Make 3 Roster Changes
The Dodgers do know that they will begin their quest for a three-peat on Saturday, October 3.
In the meantime, here are the three roster moves the team made, per the team’s transactions tracker:
“Los Angeles Dodgers activated RHP Edgardo Henriquez from the 15-day injured list.”
“Los Angeles Dodgers recalled LHP Ronan Kopp from Oklahoma City Comets.”
“Los Angeles Dodgers recalled SS Hyeseong Kim from Oklahoma City Comets.”
The most notable roster move of the trio is Edgardo Henriquez being activated from the 15-day IL, which could be a huge boost to the Dodgers’ bullpen. However, he still needs to be announced on the Dodgers’ NLDS roster, which has not been made public yet.
As for Hyeseong Kim, he could be a pinch-runner option if the Dodgers opt to go that route.
More MLB on Heavy: Chicago Cubs Announce Interesting Seiya Suzuki Decision Before MLB Playoffs
What Do Roster Moves Mean for Los Angeles Dodgers Playoff Chances?
If Henriquez can go for the Los Angeles Dodgers’ relief corps, that is a huge boost because he has been one of the team’s breakout pitchers and a highly dependable reliever.
As for the other two moves, they might not be noticeable now, but could play a role down the line.
Ronan Kopp being recalled to the 40-man roster is likely in case of an emergency, but if the Dodgers advance past the NLDS, there’s a slight chance he could be added to the official postseason roster.
Hyeseong Kim is a player who could pay slight dividends on the bases if manager Dave Roberts opts to use him in the late innings as a pinch-runner option.

ワイルドカードシリーズ第1戦【カブス0-8パドレス】サンディエゴ／ペトコパーク、9月29日（日本時間30日）
　3年連続でワイルドカードでのポストシーズン進出を果たしたパドレスは、カブスとのワイルドカードシリーズ第1戦。試合はパドレス打線が実力を発揮し、序盤からリードを奪って優勢を築く展開となった。初回にフェルナンド・タティスJr.とマニー・マチャドのホームランで2点を先制すると、中盤以降も得点を重ねた。投げては先発マイケル・キングが七回途中までノーヒットの快投で無失点。その後もリリーフ陣が無失点で繋いで8-0で勝利し、地区優勝決定シリーズ進出に王手をかけた。八回にパドレスの2番手として登板した松井裕樹は、1回1三振無失点の好リリーフ。カブス・鈴木誠也は「4番・右翼」でスタメン出場し、3打数1安打だった。
　キングは立ち上がりから見事な投球。カブスの1番ピート・クロウ＝アームストロングを直球で三球三振に仕留めると、2番アレックス・ブレグマンは外角のスイーパーで空振り三振。3番マイケル・ブッシュをファーストゴロに抑え、三者凡退と最高の出だしとなった。
　その直後、パドレスは1番タティスJr.が初球のチェンジアップを振り抜くと、打球はセンターへ。中堅手クロウ＝アームストロングのジャンプもわずかに及ばず、先頭打者ホームランで先制した。さらに3番マチャドもチェンジアップを左中間へ運び、1点を追加。パドレスは初回から2点のリードを奪った。
　さらにパドレスは三回、2死一塁からマチャドが右中間フェンス直撃のタイムリー二塁打で1点を追加。四回は7番ザンダー・ボガーツのソロ本塁打、五回には4番ジャクソン・メリルの2点タイムリーと相手のバッテリーミスでさらにリードを広げ、7点差とした。
　キングは二回以降も好投。シンカーとスイーパーのコンビネーションが冴えわたり、空振りを量産し、カブス打線を手玉に取った。得点圏に走者を背負ったのは二回の1度だけ。七回に6番ニコ・ホーナーにヒットを打たれノーヒットノーランの夢はついえたが、後続を抑えて7回1安打、8三振無失点の圧巻の投球でマウンドを降りた。
　パドレスは七回にタティスJr.が盗塁を仕掛け、悪送球でボールが転々とする間に一気にホームに生還して追加点。その後は2番手松井が八回を三者凡退。3番手マスグローブは右ひじの負傷から復活し、2024年10月2日以来2年ぶりのメジャーでの登板。かつてパドレスでノーヒットノーランを達成した経験があるベテランは、ファンの温かい声援を背に、ピンチを招きながらも無失点で試合を締めた。
　鈴木は第1打席でエラーでチーム初のランナーとして出塁。第2打席は落ち着いて四球を選んだ。第3打席はセンターフライだったが、最終回の第4打席でセンター前ヒット。次戦以降につながる打撃を見せた。

- The Chicago Cubs’ investment in innovative bat technology is part of a growing trend within the league. ($)

item.content:encoded:
A common debate that I’ve had with league executives is how many $100+-million contracts will actually be handed out this winter.
Some say one. Others say two. Others say three. But what everyone can agree on is that this is a weaker-than-usual free agent class. The clear headliner is Los Angeles Dodgers superstar Tarik Skubal; after that, industry sources have a wide range of views as to how good this group is — and who should be considered the best non-Skubal target.
I've weighed in with my own take below. Here’s a look at the top 26 free agents of the coming winter, with educated guesses as to who will (and won't) opt out of their contracts in some cases.
1. LHP Tarik Skubal
Skubal is the consensus top free agent in the class, and the expectation is that just about all of the big-market teams will be bidding on the superstar left-hander. He should top the current record for a free-agent contract given to a starting pitcher, currently held by Yoshinobu Yamamoto at $325 million. One source predicted that Skubal could try to sign before the lockout to try and get ahead of CBA uncertainty, though his agent Scott Boras is known for waiting out the market.
2. OF Seiya Suzuki
Suzuki, 32, is one of the top bats on the market and has improved defensively in the corner outfield. He’s hit at least 20 home runs in four consecutive seasons, with a career-high 32 in 2025, and will have plenty of interest from offense-needy teams — with an early report already linking the slugger to the Toronto Blue Jays.
3. OF Randy Arozarena
Arozarena is Mr. Consistent. He’s posted six consecutive 20-20 seasons and he had a very strong contract year in 2026, hitting .281/.381/.484 with 26 home runs and 79 RBI. He’s earned a multi-year deal, one that eventually should top Teoscar Hernandez’s three-year, $66 million pact with the Dodgers.
4. 3B/OF Teruaki Sato (Hanshin Tigers)
Sato, 27, is hitting .315/.392/.620 with 37 home runs and 100 RBI this season in NPB. The third baseman/outfielder is the best power hitter on the market and is in the running to win the MVP award in Japan. It’s difficult to predict what he will ultimately sign for, especially after Munataki Murakami’s surprising free agency last year, but he will have a wide market of suitors.
5. LHP Trevor Rogers
Rogers, 28, has had an up-and-down tenure with the Orioles, from being traded to the franchise in 2024 to getting optioned to the Minors after posting a 7.11 ERA in four appearances. He then had a 1.81 ERA last season and has followed it up with a 4.03 ERA this year, though he once again finished strong with a 3.52 ERA in 79.1 innings in the second half.
6. RHP Freddy Peralta
It’s been a roller-coaster year for Peralta, who once seemed like a lock to sign a nine-figure contract but strugged enough with the Mets that a one-year deal seemed plausible, if not likely. Now, he’s bounced back with the Tampa Bay Rays, posting a 3.25 ERA in 10 starts, and one league source texted recently that he “will do just fine” in free agency. One additional note: Peralta is regarded as one of the best clubhouse guys in baseball. He is universally loved by every one of his teammates, past and present.
7. C Ryan Jeffers
At one point, Jeffers felt like a lock to be traded ahead of the Aug. 3 deadline, and he ultimately stayed with the Minnesota Twins. While he’s not the best defensive catcher in baseball, his offense more than makes up for it, and he hit .256/.353/.461 with an .814 OPS, 14 home runs and 56 RBI this season. With how many teams need catching, he seems primed to turn down the qualifying offer in favor of a multi-year deal this winter.
8. RHP Michael King
King is not technically a free agent, but we’ll put him here anyway. The 31-year-old has been tremendous for the Padres with a 3.21 ERA in 32 starts. There were concerns about his durability last winter, hence why he signed an opt out-heavy contract to return to San Diego (he had an in-division offer he strongly considered, too). And it should be noted that despite those concerns, his arm has relatively little wear and tear across eight Major League seasons (just 679.2 career innings).
9. 2B Brandon Lowe
I was talking on the phone with a high-ranking rival executive recently when Lowe’s name was brought up. “He’s a f***ing beast, bro.” He’s not wrong! Lowe hit 35 home runs with 96 RBI while slashing .260/.331/.493 in his first year in Pittsburgh. What’s been most noteworthy is his improvement defensively. He’s going to do very well in free agency, with plenty of teams eagerly awaiting the chance to sign the free-agent infielder.
10. LHP Adrian Morejon
Morejon was mentioned plenty at the trade deadline, but what was not mentioned much was that the Padres and A.J. Preller love the left-hander. They did not want to part with him and mess with their bullpen unless the offer was truly too good to pass up. A return to San Diego should not be ruled out. But a player with Morejon’s production (a 2.83 ERA in 76 appearances) while only being 27 years old will have an extensive market.
11. 2B Jazz Chisholm Jr.
Chisholm Jr. had a breakout season last year with the Yankees when he hit 31 home runs. His numbers have come down a bit in 2026, with the infielder hitting .231/.312/.399 with 19 home runs and 55 RBI. Still, he’s only 28 years old, younger than Suzuki and Arozarena, and has been to the postseason four years in a row. He’ll be one of the most talked-about free agents of the offseason, but the expectation I have from talking to folks across baseball is he’ll have a good market.
12. RHP David Bednar
For years, Bednar has been one of the best relievers in baseball. He was the subject of consistent trade interest with the Pirates, who ultimately traded him to the Yankees at the 2025 deadline. He’s been very good in the Bronx, with a 2.39 ERA in 86 games since being traded. He’s proven that he can pitch in the biggest of markets, which will only bolster his value. At only 31 years old, he’s primed for a lucrative multi-year contract.
13. OF Ian Happ
Happ, 31, has been one of the most consistent players in baseball across his 10-year career. He’s hit over 21 home runs in each of the last four seasons. His numbers this year declined, however, as he hit only .218/.326/.412 with 24 home runs and 68 RBI. He’s striking out more and his OPS+ finished at 103, noticeably lower than his career average of 114.
14. LHP Foster Griffin
Griffin was perhaps the steal of the offseason, with the Washington Nationals signing the left-hander for one year and $5.5 million. He posted a 3.06 ERA in 22 starts with the Nats and was eventually traded to the Guardians for multiple prospects at the deadline. He finished the year with a 3.60 ERA in 31 starts, and is in line for a multi-year contract this winter. He’s been a tremendous success story coming after coming back from pitching in Japan for three seasons.
15. 2B Luis Arraez
Arraez has always been one of the best hitters in baseball; his defense has been what has given teams hesitation. Those concerns are no more as he’s morphed into an above-average second baseman after working with Ron Washington in San Francisco. If healthy, he’ll have a real chance at a multi-year contract this offseason after slashing .310/.345/.419 with an .801 OPS.
16. RHP Sonny Gray
Gray is not technically a free agent, but he has a $30 million mutual option. Mutual options are never picked up, though, and if he becomes available, he will be heavily in demand — and a contract in the three-year, $75 million range would make plenty of sense. But he did recently tell Chris Cotillo of MassLive.com that he would retire “in a heartbeat” if his family indicated a desire for him to hang up his cleats. He clearly still has more in the tank, but this will be a situation to monitor that could affect the rest of the pitching market.
17. RHP Casey Mize
Mize, 29, appeared primed for a lucrative multi-year contract earlier this season when he had a 2.70 ERA in 16 starts with the Detroit Tigers. Since being traded to the San Diego Padres, he has a 7.46 ERA and a 25/19 strikeout-to-walk ratio. He could be a strong candidate for a short-term deal so he can have a better platform season and hit the market again after 2027 in hopes for a long-term contract.
18. LHP Robbie Ray
Ray, 34, is surely looking at a short-term contract at this stage of his career. He was consistent with the Giants, with a 3.54 ERA in 60 starts, but has struggled with the Padres to the tune of a 5.02 ERA (5.14 FIP). He’s proven durable the last couple seasons after missing significant time in 2023 and 2024 and can be a valuable innings-eater in the bottom half of the rotation. He won’t command top dollar, but any team who signs him will be very happy.
19. RHP Kevin Gausman
Parting with Gausman was very, very difficult for the Blue Jays. He’s been the model of consistency and durability, with the right-hander pitching at least 31 games in each season since 2021. His numbers declined this year, with a 4.51 ERA in 32 starts, though his 3.74 FIP paints a better picture. At 35 years old, he’s looking at a short-term contract. He’s still highly regarded in baseball circles and will have plenty of suitors.
20. RHP Clay Holmes
The amount of teams after Holmes at the trade deadline was massivem and had it not been for a failed physical involving a prospect, he would have been dealt to the Arizona Diamondbacks instead. He fits perfectly behind the Cubs’ elite infield defense, and considering that he is no longer eligible for the qualifying offer, his value has only increased. His market will once again be substantial.
21. OF Daulton Varsho
Varsho’s value comes with his defense in center field; he’s one of the best defenders in all of baseball. He showed growth offensively last season with the Blue Jays, with a career-high 121 OPS+. But he regressed this season, with a 76 OPS+ in 2026, including a 51 OPS+ in 41 games with the Houston Astros after being traded at the deadline.
22. INF JP Crawford
Crawford feels like a near-certainty to leave the Mariners in free agency. He’s been a mainstay in the infield the last eight seasons, with his best year coming in 2023 when he posted a 5.2 bWAR. His numbers dropped this season, as he slashed only .221/.335/.352 with a .687 OPS, 14 home runs and 40 RBI.
23. RHP Hiromi Itoh, Hokkaido Nippon-Ham Fighters
Itoh, 29 in August, posted a 3.18 ERA in 172.2 innings. He has a seven-pitch arsenal and a fastball that touches 96 mph. He won the Sawamura Award in NPB, similar to the Cy Young Award, and teams have gotten a look at him in each of the last two World Baseball Classics.
24. RHP Dustin May
May, a former top prospect, has all the tools in his body. He has plenty of fans across baseball and there are some who believe he can still be a difference-maker atop a rotation — hence the Cardinals’ one year, $12.5 million contract for the right-hander in the offseason and the Milwaukee Brewers’ midseason trade for him. He’s since posted a 4.70 ERA in 31 starts, with a 3.63 FIP. A short-term contract once again feels likely for May.
25. OF Trent Grisham
Grisham, 29, accepted the qualifying offer last winter to stay with the Yankees for another season. While he broke out in 2025 with 34 home runs and 74 RBI, he came back down to earth with a .211/.308/.395 slash line with 18 home runs and 59 RBI this year. His 95 OPS+ puts him slightly below league-average this season. He feels like a candidate to once again sign a short-term deal in free agency.
26. 1B/OF Jake Bauers
Bauers has been a revelation in Milwaukee, and there is a real conversation to be had here about a potential qualifying offer. He’s hit .266/.389/.484 with 26 home runs and 86 RBI, and has emerged as a favorite of manager Pat Murphy, who recently noted that the slugger is being pitched to like one of the top hitters in baseball.
Honorable mentions: RHP Nick Martinez, C Carson Kelly, OF Taylor Ward, DH Joc Pederson, RHP Raisel Iglesias, OF/DH George Springer, RHP Jack Flaherty, RHP Tyler Mahle, LHP Kris Bubic,1B Ty France

item.content:encoded:
The best time of the baseball year is finally here. The playoffs begin Tuesday, with a quadruple-header of wild-card games on tap. The schedule for each series' first two games is identical.
Let's break down how each team got here, how they can win, X-factors, series predictions and more before the wild-card round begins.
AL: CWS-HOU • BOS-NYY | NL: PHI-ATL • CHC-SD
No. 6 Philadelphia Phillies vs. No. 3 Atlanta Braves
Projected starters
(all times ET)
Game 1, 2 p.m. Tuesday (NBC/PCK): Jesús Luzardo (PHI) vs. Chris Sale (ATL)
Game 2, 2 p.m. Wednesday (NBC/PCK): Cristopher Sánchez (PHI) vs. Tyler Mahle (ATL)
Game 3, TBD*: Aaron Nola (or Zack Wheeler on four days' rest) (PHI) vs. Grant Holmes (ATL)
(*if necessary)
How they got here
Phillies: It was a Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde type of season for the Phillies, to say the least. For the second time in five seasons, an in-season managerial firing was needed to light a fire under an underperforming veteran roster that appeared to be letting their window close. But the Phillies, like they've done before, found a way to get themselves going on the back of their starting rotation. The Phillies didn't make it easy on themselves in September, going 10-14 down the stretch and needing to win their regular-season finale against the Rays to punch their ticket to the postseason. But now that they're in, this veteran group will look to show that they're better than the past month suggests.
Braves: It was a reassuring year in Atlanta, a much-needed reminder that no, this era of Braves baseball was not over after their disastrous, postseason-less 2025. A change in manager, from the now-retired Brian Snitker to the endearingly pugnacious Walt Weiss, set the tone. As did a major refresh of Atlanta's coaching staff. That turnover, in contrast with the continuity on the roster, proved crucial as Atlanta waltzed to its first division title since 2023.
Big campaigns from metronomic first baseman Matt Olson and 2025 NL Rookie of the Year Drake Baldwin shocked nobody. The same was true for ace Chris Sale, certain to be voted an NL Cy Young finalist. But few would've predicted Michael Harris II leading the team in bWAR with a dynamic, consistent offensive season. Role players such as Mauricio Dubón, Mike Yastrzemski and Dominic Smith all delivered critical production to help offset underwhelming seasons from the likes of Ozzie Albies and Austin Riley.
Ronald Acuña Jr., that wonderfully mercurial burst of baseballing light, might've fit into that last group if not for an otherworldly September in which he clocked seven homers with a .950 OPS. That renaissance continuing into October would be a game-changer for the Braves, whose 2021 title came with Acuña sidelined.
X-factors
Phillies: Trea Turner
The regular season wasn't kind to shortstop Trea Turner, who recorded the worst season of his career. But the thing about the postseason is that it allows players who have not yet written the final story on their season to become heroes. And if the Phillies want to move past Atlanta and reach the NLDS for the fifth straight year, Turner finding his rhythm would be a welcomed sight for the team's offense. Turner has a .733 OPS off Sale in 25 career at-bats and a very respectable .863 OPS off Mahle in 25 career at-bats.
Braves: Tyler Mahle
Chris Sale is going to start Game 1 for Atlanta, and he's probably going to be pretty good. That feels as bankable as anything in our topsy-turvy world. But Mahle, set to throw Game 2, has been one of the game's most reliable starters since he joined the Braves from a zip-less San Francisco team at the deadline. The veteran righty posted a 1.99 ERA with Atlanta, allowing one earned or fewer in seven of his nine starts.
Mahle's most recent start, however, was a relative stinker. He surrendered five runs and struck out just four at home against an undermanned Reds lineup. And the underlying metrics, it should be said, are a bit more skeptical about Mahle's prospects. That's understandable. He doesn't throw that hard or strike out oodles of hitters. He hasn't conjured more swing-and-miss or meaningfully lowered opponents' hard-hit rate as a Brave. And yet, Mahle has found a way to find outs. Whether he can do so against Philly's bats will be huge.
How they win
Phillies: Can any team in baseball go toe-to-toe with Philly's starting rotation? With the quartet of Wheeler, Sánchez, Luzardo and Nola, the Phillies should have the advantage in a three-, five- or seven-game series. So while their offense is more of a wild card (pun intended), this team should be able to count on its starter giving them a chance to win every time out. And if that foursome gets hot, it's not outlandish to believe they could carry Philly on another deep postseason run.
Braves: It has been a restful week for the Braves, who were able to sit back, relax and line up their starting rotation for this wild-card series. The same cannot be said for Philly, which needed every last out to clinch on the regular season's final day. For the Phillies, the sense of exhaustion is real and gives Atlanta a legitimate advantage.
But it all starts with Sale. If he cruises like he's capable of in Game 1, that puts Atlanta in the catbird seat. Only one team in the current playoff format (the 2025 Yankees) came back to win a wild-card series after losing the first game.
Series prediction: Braves in 3

Game 2 5 p.m. ET Wednesday (PCK/NBCSN): Sean Burke (CWS) vs. Hunter Brown (HOU)
Game 3, TBD*: Davis Martin (CWS) vs. Hayden Wesneski (HOU)
(*if necessary)
How they got here
White Sox: The White Sox have been easily one of the best stories of the 2026 regular season, reaching the postseason for the first time since 2021. Chicago became the first team in MLB history to reach the postseason following three consecutive 100-loss seasons, capturing the third AL wild-card spot. The offense, led by first-time All-Stars Miguel Vargas and Munetaka Murakami, was the driving force behind the Sox's success. Chicago finished the season with a top-five offense in MLB.
The fact that the White Sox didn't win the AL Central might come as a disappointment, considering they were in first place for the majority of the second half. Still, it's undeniable that any result that puts them in the playoffs is a huge victory for the organization and a fan base that has been waiting for competitive baseball.
Astros: For a franchise that has accomplished so much over the past decade, there's something shameful, even humiliating about raising the 2026 AL West banner. That's because these Astros are, by record, the single worst division winner in the sport's long past. Before Sunday, no team with a .500 record or below had ever reached the postseason. But Houston rewrote history thanks to an MVP-caliber season from Yordan Alvarez and a tidal wave of mediocrity from its AL West counterparts. Their inclusion in the October jamboree is more an indictment of the Texas Rangers and the Seattle Mariners than anything else, but the Astros at least ended on a high note with their 9-0 win over the A's on Sunday.
Houston also deserves a morsel of credit for refurbishing its season after a disastrous April. Reaching .500 with the fourth-worst starting staff by ERA — only the Reds, A's and Rockies were worse — is also an accomplishment worth commending, a testament to something. Where would this club be without Peter Lambert, whose 3.87 ERA in 153 2/3 innings offered the only semblance of stability for a roster constantly in flux?
Things got sad enough, discombobulated enough, that in August owner Jim Crane relieved GM Dana Brown of his duties. There's an overwhelming expectation that skipper Joe Espada won't be back next year, either. It's difficult to be optimistic about Houston's very uncertain future. But in the random present of playoff baseball, anything is possible — especially when you employ the best hitter on the planet.
X-factors
White Sox: Munetaka Murakami
Munetaka Murakami is a game-changer, and his presence in the White Sox's lineup is a huge advantage in the postseason. The White Sox's rookie slugger burst onto the scene in 2026, hitting 35 home runs and providing instant impact in his first season after coming over from Japan. But following a midseason hamstring injury, the league seemed to adjust to him; Murakami finished with a slashline of .184/.328/.423 and 11 homers since Aug 1. Still, he has the type of power that can change a series by himself, and with three homers in the final week of the season, he appears to be coming out of his second-half slump. If Murakami has rediscovered his power stroke, it could change this series.
Astros: Isaac Paredes
Yordan Alvarez is currently the best hitter on earth. He cannot, under any circumstances, be allowed to dictate proceedings during this series. Chicago must make somebody else in Houston's mediocre lineup beat them. If there's a base open with Alvarez up, he should just stroll straight to first every time.
That puts a mountain of pressure on Paredes. The stocky third baseman has been hitting right behind Alvarez for most of the season and has, for the most part, showed well. He's a supremely weird hitter, one who rarely hits the ball hard or barrels it up. But Paredes doesn't whiff, doesn't punch out and has a preternatural knack for pulling the ball in the air. Expect him to come up multiple times in big spots with runners on.
How they win
White Sox: The White Sox's offense has carried them all season, and if they hope to advance to the ALDS against their division rival, they'll have to slug their way there. Vargas, Murakami and shortstop Colson Montgomery each finished the season with more than 30 longballs, and the Sox finished fifth in MLB in homers. For a team built to slug, Daikin Park in Houston isn't the worst environment to play in on the road. Chicago's power-packed lineup has shown that if they're hitting the ball out of the ballpark, offensively, they can play with anyone.
Astros: Houston desperately needs offensive contributions from someone besides Alvarez. Maybe it's the aforementioned Paredes or the en fuego Yainer Díaz. Perhaps Jose Altuve, 36 years old and in full decline, has one magical month left in his Hall of Fame career. But with such a tattered pitching staff, the Astros need to score to win. They also need to win the Hunter Brown start; he's far and away their best starter. They need a lot, frankly. And yet, much weirder October things have happened inside that East Texas thunderdome over the past decade.

No. 5 Boston Red Sox vs. No. 4 New York Yankees

(all times ET)
Game 1, 8 p.m. Tuesday (NBC/PCK): Payton Tolle (BOS) vs. Cam Schlittler (NYY)
Game 2, 8 p.m. Wednesday (NBC/PCK): Sonny Gray (BOS) vs. Max Fried (NYY)
Game 3, TBD*: Ranger Suárez (BOS) vs. Gerrit Cole (NYY)

How they got here
Red Sox: Odysseus would be proud. What a winding, bizarre and tumultuous road it has been for the Sox. Boston began the year like a snail on Unisom, posting a lackluster 9-17 record through April 24. That precipitated a dramatic, Red Wedding-style culling, in which manager Alex Cora and several other staff members were relieved of their duties. Extended injury list stints for the team's two most important pieces, outfielder Roman Anthony and 2025 Cy Young runner-up Garrett Crochet, made a turnaround feel awfully unlikely. On July 24, the Sox lost a rubber match in Colorado and traveled home 14 games under .500. Their postseason odds wallowed around 10%.
Then, everything changed. It began with a home mop against the Yanks and fully kicked into gear when the Red Sox hit the road for a three-city swing the first week of July. They went 9-0 on that trip before winning six straight at home. That 15-game streak catapulted them back into contention and the good graces of an understandably unplugged fan base. Between July 3 and Aug. 7, the Sox went a ridiculous 32-5, trampolining from 14 games under .500 to 13 games over. Fenway was a zoo. Nothing could go wrong. Boston ballfans beamed once again.
The heater earned Cora's replacement, Chad Tracy, the full-time gig. It also afforded the Sox a relatively comfortable September. It's worth noting, though, that Boston has not played particularly crisply since cooling off from the volcanic run, with a 21-22 record since Aug. 8. Ultimately, their final numbers and standing in the American League are not shocking or unexpected, even though Boston's odyssey was wonky beyond comparison.
Yankees: For all the stress, the drama, the hand-wringing, for all the injuries and under-performance, 2026 was a relatively straightforward season in YankeeLand. A lot, it should be said, went wrong. Reigning AL MVP Aaron Judge has played just seven games since May. Giancarlo Stanton hasn't played since April. Max Fried and Carlos Rodón each missed about two months. Young players such as Anthony Volpe, Jasson Dominguez and Austin Wells regressed offensively. Gerrit Cole, coming back from Tommy John, didn't fully recapture his frontline best.
And yet, here the Yankees are, with 93 wins and in an identical place to where they finished last year. That's thanks to breakout campaigns from homegrown pieces such as Cam Schlittler (the AL Cy Young favorite) and Ben Rice (41 home runs and a .897 OPS). Closer David Bednar has been dynamite. Cody Bellinger has been a rock. Skipper Aaron Boone kept the train on the tracks. Three games at home against the Red Sox await. Beyond that looms an ALDS against a daunting division foe. We've been here before.
The largest difference, of course, is the uncertainty swirling around Judge. The Yankees' captain missed three months due to a rib problem, came back for a week, strained his calf and went back on the shelf. Boone says he's preparing for a wild-card round without Judge. Judge says he plans to play. What sort of magic this reduced version of Judge can conjure is easily the juiciest storyline ahead of this rivalry showdown. That said, this series, like this Yankees season, is probably going to be dictated by the pitchers.
X-factors
Red Sox: Roman Anthony
It has been an odd season for the 22-year-old, who missed last year's wild-card festivities due to injury. In March, Anthony was a late addition to Team USA's WBC roster. He shined on that grand stage, impressing his more established teammates and earning plaudits from a coaching staff of hardball lifers. That only ratcheted up the hype on a player expected to carry a franchise less than a year after he became legally permitted to drink a beer.
So when Anthony started slowly, disappointment bubbled. Then, on May 4, he tore a ligament in his finger; that kept him out of action until Aug. 30. A lot happened in the interim, most of which Anthony spent rehabbing at the team's complex in Florida. Since returning, he has looked promising, tantalizingly close to unleashing the full assortment of his talents upon the league. Now, with Willson Contreras banged up and either unavailable or restricted, the pressure returns to Anthony's young shoulders.
Yankees: Luis García Jr.
García was a curious character for the Yankees to shape their trade deadline around. Instead of acquiring a piece that filled an obvious void (righty stick with defensive value or versatility), GM Brian Cashman opted to add the most dynamic hitter possible. New York landed on García, who was in the midst of an offensive breakout under a new Washington Nationals regime.
For a month, that plan bore fruit, with the Dominican slugger posting an .846 OPS in August. But since then, the wheels have fallen off, with García's chase rate skyrocketing. His September OPS started with a 5. He has homered just twice since Aug. 26. He doesn't have an extra-base hit since Sept. 10. There's a chance, given Boston's bevy of southpaws and New York's DH surplus, that he doesn't start every game. But García will get his chances, and whether he comes up big might swing the series.
How they win
Red Sox: Boston's pitching staff is the only one in baseball that ranks in the top five in both home run rate and walk rate. That's a rare combo. Usually, throwing the ball in the strike zone more often leads to more hard contact. But these Red Sox hurlers, for whatever reason, have threaded that needle perfectly. No team in the league has allowed fewer homers. However, no team has hit more than the Yankees. Boston revitalized its season behind pitching and defense, keeping the scores low and the games close. Doing so here will give them the best chance of authoring an upset.
Yankees: No American League team can compete with New York's starting staff. But the Yankees need more than dominance from Schlittler, Fried and Cole. They need length. The bridge to Bednar is unsteady. So the longer the starters go, the rosier that path looks. Offensively, the Yankees need a big swing or two from their right-handed bats against Boston's left-handed arms. That could come from a banged-up Judge or Stanton. It could come from veteran southpaw-killer Paul Goldschmidt, trade-acquisition Heliot Ramos or rookie shortstop George Lombard Jr. If it comes from the beleaguered Anthony Volpe, the tri-state area will lose its collective marbles. But somebody, anybody who stands on the right side of the batter's box has to make an impact.
Series prediction: Yankees in 3
No. 5 Chicago Cubs vs. No. 4 San Diego Padres
(all times ET)
Projected starters
Game 1, 10 p.m. Tuesday (PCK/NBCSN): Shota Imanaga (CHC) vs. Michael King (SD)
Game 2, 10 p.m. Wednesday (PCK/NBCSN): Clay Holmes (CHC) vs. Nick Pivetta (SD)
Game 3, TBD*: Matthew Boyd (CHC) vs. Walker Buehler or Casey Mize or Robbie Ray (SD)

How they got here
Cubs: It was Pete Crow-Armstrong's world, and the rest of us just lived in it. Chicago's 24-year-old center fielder went fully supersonic this year, cranking 45 homers, swiping 41 bags and delivering a .945 OPS with his typically elite outfield defense. He will win the NL MVP, and it might be unanimous. That performance shaped and guided and defined this Cubs' season, electrifying an offense that led baseball in OPS, K/BB rate and runs per game.
Alex Bregman's arrival via free agency, too, cannot be understated. He struggled mightily for the first few months, with his extended schneid at one point eliciting boos from a frustrated Wrigley crowd. But since July 12, Bregman leads all qualified National League hitters in OPS. His experience, comportment and leadership, by all accounts, have also had a meaningful impact on Crow-Armstrong.
But pitching woes, in both the rotation and the bullpen, kept Chicago from ever seriously threatening the Brewers for the NL Central title. The Cubs started the year on something of a roller coaster, with two 10-game winning streaks and a 10-game losing streak before the calendar flipped to June. They'll enter October on something of an ice floe, with 15 runs scored in their final six contests.
Padres: San Diego has the best record in baseball since July 24. The day before, the Pads lost a rubber match in Atlanta to fall to three games under. 500. That pushed the club four games adrift of a wild-card spot, with the Cardinals, Pirates, Marlins, Nationals and Diamondbacks standing between them and a trip to October. That was the low-water mark for this team.
Since that date, the Padres have gone 41-18. They won five straight in late July, six straight in August and eight straight in September. They've lost thrice since Labor Day. The reason for the resurgence? Check out these numbers.
| Padres offensive ranks before and after July 24 | | |
| | Before | After |
| Runs/game | 4.14 (25th) | 4.95 (3rd) |
| AVG | .230 (28th) | .268 (2nd) |
| OBP | .307 (27th) | .339 (2nd) |
| SLG | .383 (27th) | .425 (2nd) |
| OPS | .689 (26th) | .764 (2nd) |
San Diego's offense went from bottom-five to top-five. Some of that is batted-ball luck and sequencing. A lot of it is Fernando Tatis Jr. turning back into a monster. Jackson Merrill had a similar rebirth. Ty France continued his bounce-back campaign. Xander Bogaerts shifted from unwatchable to capable. Unsung heroes such as Dustin Harris and Luis Rengifo got hot. The starting pitching did just enough. The game's best bullpen never stopped dominating. It's that unit, led by a cadre of flamethrowers in Mason Miller, Adrian Morejon and Bradgley Rodriguez, that makes these Padres a particularly formidable October opponent.
X-factors
Cubs: Alex Bregman — specifically, his face
One week ago, Bregman was the victim of some very painful misfortune. A check-swing foul ball off the bat of Cubs first baseman Michael Busch struck Bregman in the face while he was standing in the on-deck circle. Blood dripped from below his left eye as he scurried down the dugout steps into the clubhouse. A trip to the hospital revealed multiple facial fractures. The incident kept Bregman out of the lineup until Friday, when he went 0-for-4 with a strikeout as Chicago's DH. He went 4-for-4 with two home runs and a walk in Sunday's season finale.
There's no doubt that Bregman, the textbook definition of a "grinder," will take the field in October. But at what level? He has been so integral to Chicago's lineup for the past few months that even a slightly reduced version of Bregman could unsettle things. Among active players, only his former Astros teammate Jose Altuve has taken more postseason plate appearances.
Padres: Fernando Tatis Jr.
Nothing is more meaningfully different about this year's Padres team compared to the one that went three and see-ya at Wrigley in 2025 than Fernando Tatis Jr.'s stunning offensive reemergence. Things didn't start so swimmingly this year for the swaggering outfielder, who needed 55 games to clock his first longball of this season. But since May 30, Tatis' .914 OPS ranks fourth in the NL, and his 4.9 fWAR ranks second in MLB behind only Crow-Armstrong.
This version of Tatis looks a lot like the one who took the baseball world by storm en route to finishing third in NL MVP in 2021. Will that brilliance show up in a small October sample? It usually has throughout the 27-year-old's career; he holds a 1.114 postseason OPS in 70 plate appearances. Tatis, though, has never advanced past the NLDS. Remember, he was in PED timeout when the Padres stampeded to the NLCS in 2022. Could this month be his path back to full-blown superstardom?
How they win
Cubs: The margins were razor thin when these teams lined up in the wild-card round last year, with a highlight reel of web gems from shortstop Dansby Swanson making the difference. Those games, oddly enough, were incredibly low-scoring, with Chicago snagging two 3-1 wins and San Diego edging out a 3-0 win. It's hard to imagine the Cubs and their underwhelming relief group winning that way again, particularly on the road. To advance, they'll need buckets of runs. With PCA, Bregman, Seiya Suzuki and Co., that's a real possibility.
Padres: The Padres' formula for success has been the same for the past few seasons: Shorten the game. San Diego realistically needs five innings from its starters. Then manager Craig Stammen gets to turn things over to the best relief core in baseball, led by southpaw Adrían Morejon and flamethrower Mason Miller. The Friars' starting pitching has gotten stronger as they've gotten healthy, so if Michael King in Game 1 and likely Nick Pivetta in Game 2 can each give San Diego 15 outs, the Padres have a good chance of making quick work of Chicago.

Pete Crow-Armstrong stole his 40th base on the same afternoon the Chicago Cubs locked up a second straight playoff trip. This timing turned a historic stat line into a full-blown vindication for the front office. The 24-year-old entered the game with 45 homers and 39 steals before taking off against Tyler Phillips in the first inning.
The crowd at Wrigley Field paused to watch him reach second base. One pitch after a leadoff walk, the milestone was official. Only three players in history have hit at least 45 homers while stealing 40 bases in a single season. Crow-Armstrong is now one of them.
The Trade That Changed Everything
Look back at the 2021 trade deadline for the full picture. The Cubs sent Javier Baez and Trevor Williams to the New York Mets. In return, they got Crow-Armstrong, who was just a prospect with recent shoulder surgery. Baez was a hometown hero who helped win the 2016 World Series. Crow-Armstrong had played only six pro games before the deal. His bat was far from a sure thing at the time.
FanSided originally gave the Mets an A- for that swap while the Cubs got a B+. The writers called it a risk then. The Mets could have never imagined such a disastrous outcome for this deal, which has now deteriorated significantly. Crow-Armstrong's 40-40 season proves the Cubs took the right side of the table. They traded a rental player in a lost year for a future MVP.
More Than Just Speed and Power
The numbers go deeper than just the 40-40 club. Earlier this month, his pursuit of high fWAR brought him close to a mark untouched by any National League batter since Bonds. Seiya Suzuki hit the only home run for Chicago in the 2-1 win over the Miami Marlins. The pitching staff protected that narrow lead to seal the victory.
This win guaranteed the Cubs one of the three Wild Card spots in the National League. It marks the first time since 2015 through 2018 that the team reached consecutive postseasons. Crow-Armstrong has secured two All-Star selections and a Gold Glove award already. He signed an extension that keeps him in Chicago through the 2032 campaign.
Compare the results of that 2021 trade. Since the trade, Javier Baez has accumulated 56 homers and 40 stolen bases across 590 games. Crow-Armstrong has 45 homers and 40 steals in less than half that time.

Shota Imanaga doesn’t need anyone else’s help celebrating.
The Cubs pitcher went viral after repeatedly blasting himself in the face with beer during the team’s wild clubhouse celebration after clinching a spot in the postseason Thursday.
Naturally, Imanaga had an explanation for the madness.
“This is Japanese style,” Imanaga said while holding a bottle in each hand. “Japanese misogi.”
Imanaga then turned both bottles toward himself and sprayed the beer directly onto his head and face, bobbing up and down into the streams as his teammates laughed around him.
“Self-service!” Imanaga said.
The Cubs leaned into the moment themselves, posting the video on social media captioned: “Who needs bottle service when you have self-service?”
During an interview with Marquee Sports Network’s Taylor McGregor amid the clubhouse celebration, Imanaga was showered with champagne by his teammates.
His response?
“Yummy!”
Chicago officially punched its postseason ticket with a 2-1 victory over the Marlins at Wrigley Field, securing a playoff berth for the second consecutive season.
Seiya Suzuki tied the game with his 26th home run of the season in the fifth inning before Nico Hoerner drove home Ian Happ for the eventual winning run in the sixth.
Pete Crow-Armstrong also stole his 40th base of the season in the victory, giving him 40 home runs and 40 stolen bases and making him just the seventh player in MLB history to accomplish the feat.
Imanaga has played his part in getting Chicago back to the playoffs for the second consecutive season.
The 33-year-old left-hander went 11-10 with a 3.74 ERA while remaining a fixture in Chicago’s starting rotation throughout the season.
He also recorded 171 strikeouts in 173 ⅓ innings pitched in 2026.
Last year, the Cubs went 92-70 and took care of the Padres in the wild-card round before falling to the Brewers in five games in the NLDS.
Imanaga, who was an All-Star two seasons ago, turned 33 earlier this month and has a career 3.44 ERA and a 35-21 record.

item.content:encoded:
２連覇中の世界一軍団を押しのけ、〝最恐打線〟の座に躍り出たのはシカゴの名門球団だった。
米有力紙「ニューヨーク・タイムズ」傘下のスポーツ専門サイト「ジ・アスレチック」は、２５日（日本時間同日）の段階でポストシーズン（ＰＳ）進出確率が１０％以上ある１３球団の打線を１位から１３位まで独自にランキング。得点力、長打、走力、選球眼、三振率に加え、左右投手への対応力や後半戦の内容まで洗い出した〝忖度なし〟の評価で、トップに立ったのが鈴木誠也外野手（３２）のカブスだ。
カブスは１試合平均５・３１得点、２１７本塁打、１０９盗塁、四球率１０・６％と、パワーだけでなく足と出塁力も兼備。中でもＰＣＡことピート・クロウ＝アームストロング外野手（２４）は文句なしにＭＶＰ筆頭候補級の働きで、記事ではｗＲＣ＋（（打者の得点創出力を平均１００で示す指標）１５８、ｆＷＡＲ（（打撃、走塁、守備を総合して勝利への貢献度を示す指標）１０・６と突出した数字を紹介した。鈴木もｆＷＡＲ４・３で主力の一角を担い、ロースター１４野手のうち１１人がリーグ平均を上回るｗＲＣ＋を記録。上位だけでなく、どこからでも得点の糸口をつくれる層の厚さが１位評価の決め手となった。
しかもカブスは２４日（同２５日）のマーリンズ戦を２―１で制し、２年連続のＰＳ進出を決定。ＰＣＡは４５本塁打に加えて４０盗塁へ到達し、鈴木も本塁打を放った。短期決戦を目前に、ランキングを裏付ける形で打線が存在感を示した格好だ。
一方、前年世界一のドジャースは２位。大谷翔平投手（３２）が負傷者リスト（ＩＬ）から復帰し、周囲の主力も上向いている点は高く評価されたが、シーズン全体では得点４位、本塁打９位。大谷も前半戦ＯＰＳ０・９５３に対し後半戦は０・７９５と落としており、「どこまで万全に戻っているか」が最大の焦点に挙げられた。豪華メンバーとＰＳ経験では申し分ないが、現時点の総合打力ではカブスに一歩譲る判定となった。
５年ぶりのＰＳ進出を決めた村上宗隆内野手（２６）のホワイトソックスは６位。３０本塁打以上を３人そろえ、ア・リーグ最多得点を生んだ破壊力は本物だ。その反面、三振率２４・２％は対象１３球団で２番目に高く、若手中心の打線が短期決戦でこの弱点をどう抑えるかが課題となる。ホワイトソックスは２４日にロイヤルズを９―１で下し、２０２１年以来となる「ＰＳ切符」を手にしている。
名前の重さならドジャース、勢いならホワイトソックスも引けを取らない。それでも「１位カブス、２位ドジャース、６位ホワイトソックス」と並べた容赦ない序列は、１０月の打線に問われるのが単なるネームバリューのみのスターの数ではなく、相手投手に切れ目なく圧力をかけ続ける総合力であることを浮き彫りにしている。

item.content:encoded:
Field Level Media

25 Sep 2026, 02:35 GMT+10

(Photo credit: Matt Marton)
Nico Hoerner ripped a go-ahead RBI single in the sixth and Matthew Boyd tossed seven strong innings, helping the host Chicago Cubs clinch a playoff berth with a 2-1 victory over the Miami Marlins on Thursday afternoon.
Chicago's Pete Crow-Armstrong walked to lead off the first inning and promptly stole second base to become the seventh player in MLB history to record at least 40 homers and 40 stolen bases in a single season. Armstrong, who has 45 homers, joined Jose Canseco (1988), Barry Bonds (1996), Alex Rodriguez (1998), Alfonso Soriano (2006), Ronald Acuna Jr. (2023) and Shohei Ohtani (2024) as the only players to reach the 40-40 milestone.
Seiya Suzuki belted a solo homer in the fifth inning to highlight his two-hit performance for the Cubs (88-71), who salvaged the finale of their three-game series with Miami.
Boyd (10-5) allowed one run on five hits to record his second straight victory following a 0-4 stretch over his previous six starts.
Daniel Palencia bridged the gap to Ryan Zeferjahn, who retired the side in order in the ninth inning to secure his seventh save of the season.
Jakob Marsee had an RBI single in the third inning for the Marlins (78-81), who have lost four of their last six games.
With the game tied 1-1, Ian Happ tripled off Jack Ralston (0-2) to lead off the sixth inning and came home on Hoerner's RBI single to left field.
Ralston permitted two runs on three hits in 1 1/3 innings.
Brian Navarreto doubled to lead off the third inning against Matthew Boyd before coming home on Marsee's RBI single to center to open the scoring.
Suzuki forged a tie in the fifth inning, depositing a 1-0 pitch from Ralston over the wall in center field. The homer was Suzuki's 26th of the season and second in his last four games.
--Field Level Media

Pete Crow-Armstrong became the seventh player in Major League Baseball history to achieve 40 home runs with 40 stolen bases in a single season on Thursday.
The Chicago Cubs center fielder got on a base with a leadoff walk on seven pitches against Miami Marlins starter Tyler Phillips. He took off for the milestone steal on Phillips' first pitch to the next batter, Seiya Suzuki.
Crow-Armstrong came into Thursday's matchup versus the Miami Marlins with 45 home runs, tied for the MLB lead. He reached the 40-homer mark on Sept. 6, also against the Marlins. At the time, he had 33 steals with 18 games remaining in the regular season.
This story will be updated with more information.

item.content:encoded:
Pete Crow-Armstrong is on the verge of history.
The Chicago Cubs outfielder is just one stolen base away from joining the rare 40-40 club with at least 40 home runs and 40 steals in the same season.
He surged past 40 homers a while ago now, but he still has just 39 steals through Wednesday night's game against the Miami Marlins.
PCA did have a chance to get that historic bag, though, but he slightly missed his opportunity.
PCA Chance at 40th Steal
Crow-Armstrong worked a walk in the middle of a 0-0 game against the Marlins on Wednesday.
With no one else on base, the Chicago crowd knew what it meant. Crow-Armstrong would have a chance to run.
Except, he didn't take off right away as Marlins pitcher Ryan Gusto and catcher Joe Mack worked to keep him close.
Seiya Suzuki was at the plate, but he wasn't swinging right away. With two outs in the inning of a tie game, it would benefit everyone on the Cubs for PCA to get to second base, not just for the history but for the chance of winning the game.
Despite that, Crow-Armstrong didn't take off for a few pitches. He did get Gusto to throw over twice, which meant that unless Gusto wanted to risk a balk call if PCA was safe again, he couldn't throw over a third time.
Once that happened, it seemed a foregone conclusion that Crow-Armstrong would start his engines, and he did — but the first time he took off on the pitch, he actually stopped and retreated. He must've not liked his jump. Suzuki took that pitch, but it wouldn't be a steal since Crow-Armstrong didn't keep going.
Finally, on the next pitch, Crow-Armstrong got a huge jump — but it was a two-strike offering in the zone, and Suzuki swung as he needed to, and he flew out to right field to end the inning.
Crow-Armstrong was close to history, but he didn't try to take it immediately, and the wait will go on.
Waiting Game
Crow-Armstrong sat at 37 steals for nearly a week before swiping one bag on Sunday and another on Tuesday to get to 39.
One of the tough parts of a 40-40 season is that the guys who hit at least 40 home runs often aren't starting their trips around the bases on first base. They might touch all four bags and never get a chance, or they might hit for extra bases, which makes stealing tougher than it would be to go from first to second.
PCA should get more chances, and he'll likely take one, but the mechanics of it all aren't always simple.
The other risk is if the Cubs solidify their playoff position with a game or two to play, they could always rest Crow-Armstrong to prepare for the postseason. At least as far as achieving the history goes, it'd behoove Crow-Armstrong to make it happen as soon as possible.

item.content:encoded:
Chicago Cubs fans around the country breathed a sigh of relief on Tuesday, when manager Craig Counsell sure made it sound like the team didn't expect Alex Bregman's ugly facial fracture to keep him out of the team's postseason lineup. In fact, Counsell went as far as to say the third baseman could be back in Chicago's lineup as early as this weekend.
Just 24 hours later, though ... well, let's just say we have our doubts. Wednesday afternoon brought an interview with the man himself, and while Bregman is grinning and bearing it as best he can, it's hard not to read between the lines here and wonder how exactly he'll be ready to play playoff baseball in a matter of days.
Bregman spoke to ESPN's Jesse Rogers prior to the Cubs' game against Miami, describing the fracture as "something by the nerve of my face" — adding that, as the swelling goes down, the actual fractures have become more and more painful. He did say that the pain was "fine," but, well, that's exactly what you'd expect someone of Bregman's track record to say. In reality, you need to see pretty well to hit a baseball, and even if Bregman does insist on toughing it out in October, you have to wonder what version of him Chicago will be getting.
Cubs fans probably shouldn't get their hopes up after Alex Bregman's latest injury update
From the "never a thing you want to hear an athlete say" department, Bregman also told Rogers that fluid build-up in his face is affecting him.
In a word: yikes. Again, Bregman is as tough a player as there is in the league, and he'll no doubt do everything in his power to be in the lineup when the Cubs kick off their Wild Card series (opponent TBD) next Tuesday. And to be sure, his face already visually looks a whole lot better than it did just 48 hours or so ago; give it another few days, and the swelling and bruising should subside even more.
All of which fails to reckon with the fact that Bregman has a broken bone in his face. Not just in his face, but awfully close to his left eye, the one closest to the pitcher as he steps in the box as a right-handed hitter. Less swelling is still some swelling, and there's still the pain — and, apparently, the fluids — to worry about. It seems almost unfair to expect Bregman to hit at anything like his usual level if he's having a hard time focusing on the baseball, and that should have the Cubs thinking long and hard about whether he belongs in the lineup.
Projected Cubs lineup if Alex Bregman misses Wild Card series
Of course, it's easy for me to say, and much tougher for Craig Counsell to actually execute. Not only is Bregman a veteran leader with a great deal of latitude, but his absence would leave a notable hole in the Cubs lineup.
| Player | Position |
|---|---|
| Pete Crow-Armstrong | CF |
| Seiya Suzuki | RF |
| Michael Busch | 1B |
| Ian Happ | LF |
| Nico Hoerner | 2B |
| Michael Conforto | DH |
| Dansby Swanson | SS |
| Pedro Ramirez | 3B |
| Carson Kelly | C |
Pedro Ramirez and Matt Shaw are both exciting, versatile young players, but installing them as an every-day third baseman for a playoff series feels like asking a lot. Both are just league-average hitters, and because of Bregman's iron-man tendencies, neither has a ton of third-base experience this year (though Shaw played there a bunch last season).
Chicago does have plenty of firepower around them, in the form of pending NL MVP Pete Crow-Armstrong, Seiya Suzuki, Michael Busch and others. But Bregman has been scorching hot for pretty much the entire second half, and losing his bat would be a devastating blow to a lineup that would suddenly start to look pretty top-heavy — especially with Dansby Swanson just making his way back from an oblique injury.

item.content:encoded:
Chicago Cubs third baseman Alex Bregman, who suffered multiple facial fractures on the left side when he was struck by a foul ball while in the on-deck circle during Sunday's game, will not go on the injured list and in fact could return as soon as this coming weekend in Boston, manager Craig Counsell told reporters on Tuesday.
"I think Alex is going to be fine," he said (via ESPN). "He's planning on playing."
The fluke injury occurred when Michael Busch hit a check swing foul ball Bregman's way in the fourth inning. Bregman simply did not have enough time to react given his proximity to home plate. He shared an update on social media Monday morning:
Alex Bregman shared another update to his IG story this morning of how his face is looking after getting hit with the foul ball yesterday:
[image or embed]
Other than pain tolerance, the biggest question is whether the swelling will subside soon enough so that Bregman can see out of his left eye. If his vision is impaired, he won't be able to play. There's pretty much no way around that. Given Counsell's comments on Tuesday, it seems like maybe the swelling reduction has made good progress.
Only six days remain in the regular season. In not placing Bregman on the injured list, it shows the Cubs are hopeful that, at a bare minimum, Bregman would be available for the Wild Card Series. Chicago is five games up on a wild-card spot and can clinch a postseason berth as early as Tuesday with a win over the Marlins or a loss by the Diamondbacks. They have been eliminated from the NL Central race.
As things stand headed into Tuesday's slate, the Cubs are lined up to face the Padres, though the NL wild-card race seeding is still up in the air.
If Bregman is unable to play in the Wild Card Series, some combination of Matt Shaw and Pedro Ramírez would likely fill in, though that certainly would be a downgrade. Instead, the Cubs would have to rely more heavily on National League MVP frontrunner Pete Crow-Armstrong, Seiya Suzuki, Dansby Swanson, Nico Hoerner and others.
Bregman, 32, is hitting .262/.352/.452 with 26 home runs this season. He has 19 homers in his last 61 games and has been Chicago's second-best player behind Crow-Armstrong. This is the first year of Bregman's five-year, $175 million contract with the Cubs.

item.content:encoded:
It’s time for both sides of this great baseball town to come together.
No, not the fans. We know better than to ask for that.
Rather, we mean the Cubs and White Sox themselves, for — a doff of the cap and a drumroll, please — the Sun-Times’ 2026 All-City Team is here.
Beat writers Vinnie Duber (Cubs) and James Fegan (Sox) joined frequent baseball scribe Jeff Agrest and yours truly in selecting a 17-man team: one player at each position in the field, a designated hitter, four starting pitchers, three relievers — one of them designated as closer — and a manager.
Four ironclad rules guided our process:
1. This is a 2026 honor. Reputation doesn’t matter.
2. If it’s too close to call at certain positions, lean into which players we’d rather write into a playoff lineup.
3. All players must appear at their primary positions. No exceptions!
4. OK, fine, Alex Bregman and Miguel Vargas both need to be in there somehow. Besides, if we journalists followed the rules, how would everybody know to hate us?
Our team:
SP1: Sean Burke, Sox
Leads Chicago starters in ERA, strikeouts, opponent batting average — closest we’ve got to an ace.
SP2: Shota Imanaga, Cubs
Other than the gopher balls — so many gopher balls — lefty has been effective.
SP3: Davis Martin, Sox
Sox were 10-1 over his first 11 starts. Finishing kick has been strong, too. (As for in between, don’t ask.)
SP4: Matthew Boyd, Cubs
Still one guy who — if locked in — can get you to the seventh inning of a playoff game.
C: Carson Kelly, Cubs
Good hitter, even better with men in scoring position. Not an All-Star, but we’ll take him.
1B: Munetaka Murakami, Sox
Hamstring injury derailed spectacular start. Still, top 10 in AL in homers, walks is big-time.
2B: Chase Meidroth, Sox
Sorry, Nico Hoerner, but this was an easy call. Meidroth has simply been the better batsman.
3B: Alex Bregman, Cubs
One of the best second halves in baseball, combined with stellar glove work. Tough call, though.
SS: Dansby Swanson, Cubs
Just too great on “D” — and Colson Montgomery didn’t get on base enough to unseat him.
LF: Tristan Peters, Sox
South Side’s best outfielder — an All-Star, don’t forget — gets bumped over by you-know-who.
CF: Pete Crow-Armstrong, Cubs
But you knew this already. Not bad, Mr. MVP.
RF: Seiya Suzuki, Cubs
His RISP work wasn’t the best, but you take the offensive totals every time.
DH: Miguel Vargas, Sox
Sox’ MVP — there’s no debate about that — simply has to be in our lineup.
RP: Bryan Hudson, Sox
Quality lefty with multiple impressive scoreless streaks and pinpoint control all second half.
RP: Sean Newcomb, Sox
Lefty hangs on to a spot despite a rough September.
Closer: Grant Taylor, Sox
The best reliever in town and the only sane choice for this role.
Manager: Craig Counsell, Cubs
Potentially winning 90 despite one pitching problem after another is nothing to sneeze at.
DISSENSIONS IN THE RANKS
In the end, we were in unison on all but three positions. Fegan backed Vargas at third base and Will Venable at manager, and I wanted Sam Antonacci in left.
Fegan on Vargas: Bregman and Vargas are statistically even, so let’s get sentimental. Vargas has been the rock of a Sox offense otherwise defined by streaks. He’s the proof of concept of their newfound ability to improve hitters. A universally beloved bilingual glue guy in a loose clubhouse, Vargas is the team MVP who laughs hard and works harder. Without him, Sox leadership is talking “meaningful progress” rather than playoffs.
Greenberg on Antonacci: His defense is more mosh pit than ballet, but throw him off his spot because of it? Come on, man. He’s always on base, hits in the clutch and plays with his rear end on fire. How do you not love a young cat with a perverse desire to stand in front of 96 mph and get drilled by it? These Sox aren’t these Sox without his signature brand of — how to put it? — Antonacciness.
Fegan on Venable: His in-game moves miss the mark at times; inarguable since he readily fesses up without prompting. But with how naturally fans and commentators have shifted to second-guessing every crucial move in a division chase, it might surprise locally how well Venable does in AL manager of the year voting, or how the baseball world still views his team cracking the playoffs as coaching alchemy, or how much his constant tinkering is not unique but actually–gasp!–the Sox adhering to modern trends.
Contributing: James Fegan, Vinnie Duber, Jeff Agrest

item.content:encoded:
The Cubs are as close to securing a trip back to the postseason as possible.
The North Siders need just a single win, or a single D-backs loss, over the regular season’s final week to clinch a spot in the NL Wild Card round.
Who will the Cubs play? And where will those games be played? Those questions won’t be answered until next weekend, most likely.
But with just six games remaining until playoff baseball, who will the Cubs need to step up in order to make a run at the World Series in a National League field filled with strong contenders such as the Brewers, Dodgers and Braves?
Here’s a look at who the Cubs need to do their part to get back to the Fall Classic for the first time since 2016:
Who will step up at the back end of the 'pen?
Who will close games? This is by far the Cubs’ biggest, and potentially most important, question that needs to be answered. Will it be Jacob Webb, who leads the team with nine saves, or will former closer Daniel Palencia, who just spun two scoreless innings in one of his most impressive outings of the year, be able to take that role? Manager Craig Counsell, who has used 14 pitchers to record saves this season, will be tasked with piecing together a bullpen that has limited experience in those situations.
The Cubs need Webb, who spun a scoreless outing in 24 straight appearances from June to August, to get back into form after allowing 11 runs over his past 7 2/3 innings (nine games). If Palencia, who has thrown 6 1/3 straight scoreless innings, can also replicate his success from 2025, it could be a major boost for a club that entered Cincinnati converting just four of its past 12 save opportunities.
Deadline acquisition Ryan Zeferjahn and lefty Ryan Rolison could also play a big factor late in games, but there’s also a secret weapon waiting out in the bullpen …
Can Cabrera be a reliable relief option?
That brings us to Edward Cabrera, who returned from a recurring blister injury on his pitching hand on Sept. 15 in a multi-inning relief role. That will be his job going forward as the Cubs hope shorter outings can not only keep him healthy, but potentially provide a small uptick in velocity. Cabrera’s first relief experience had mixed results (two runs in 2 1/3 IP), but he came out of the bullpen Sunday and tossed a scoreless inning on just nine pitches.
The best-case scenario of this temporary move to the bullpen? Cabrera turns into this year’s version of the Dodgers’ Roki Sasaki, which would immediately help stabilize the back end of the Cubs’ bullpen. Cabrera’s season hasn’t gone to plan, posting a 5.68 ERA in 15 starts between three stints on the injured list, but he still has a chance to make a significant impact when it matters most.
PCA still doing MVP things in October
Is it really fair to ask more of Pete Crow-Armstrong? After going yard again Sunday, the Cubs slugger is tied with Philadelphia’s Kyle Schwarber for the most home runs in the Major Leagues. He leads Chicago in batting average (.280), homers (45), RBIs (107), stolen bases (38), runs scored (118), on-base percentage (.371), hits (170), triple (eight) and games played (156). Got all that? Simply put, he’s put together one of the most impressive offensive seasons in Cubs history and he’s not done.
But he will need others to contribute in October. While run production starts with Crow-Armstrong, even if he performs to his NL MVP front-runner ability, he can’t do it all himself. The North Siders have to count on Seiya Suzuki, Dansby Swanson, Ian Happ, Alex Bregman and Michael Busch below him in the lineup to generate scoring chances.
Holmes stepping up as playoff ace
Clay Holmes and Matthew Boyd are the clear No. 1 and No. 2 options for the playoffs, but Counsell hasn’t yet revealed who will pitch in the all-important Game 1. Holmes had a strong August (1.55 ERA in five starts) in his return to the big leagues after missing nearly three months with a right fibula fracture, but he’s allowed 16 ER in just 15 1/3 IP across three starts in September (9.39 ERA).
That’s a worrying trend for a club with limited starting options in the postseason, but Shota Imanaga has stabilized recently after a down stretch in August, and veteran Kevin Gausman can provide multiple innings in whatever role the Cubs need during the postseason.

El jardinero central de los Cubs llegó a 45 cuadrangulares y se convirtió en el primero de su posición con 40 jonrones, 30 dobles y 30 robos en una temporada.
Pete Crow-Armstrong alcanzó una combinación estadística inédita durante la contundente victoria 9-1 de los Chicago Cubs sobre los Cincinnati Reds. El jardinero terminó la jornada con tres imparables, dos carreras impulsadas, tres anotadas y una base robada.
Crow-Armstrong conectó su cuadrangular número 45 de la temporada e igualó a Kyle Schwarber en el liderato de las Grandes Ligas. También llegó a 30 dobles y 38 bases robadas, convirtiéndose en el primer jardinero central de la historia con al menos 40 jonrones, 30 dobles y 30 robos dentro de una misma campaña.
La actuación confirmó el crecimiento de un jugador capaz de influir en distintas áreas del juego. A su producción de poder agregó velocidad en las bases y una presencia constante en la ofensiva de Chicago, que se mantiene en plena lucha por asegurar su lugar en la postemporada.
Michael Conforto y Seiya Suzuki también conectaron cuadrangulares por los Cubs. Desde el montículo, David Peterson limitó a Cincinnati a una carrera y tres imparables durante seis entradas. La única anotación de los Reds llegó mediante un jonrón de JJ Bleday.
Chicago continúa entre los principales aspirantes a los comodines de la Liga Nacional. Los Cubs comparten la parte alta de esa clasificación con San Diego, mientras Filadelfia se mantiene cerca después de vencer 7-2 a los Mets.
